The double cover $\widetilde{A}_4 \twoheadrightarrow A_4$ is the *binary tetrahedral group* of order 24, isomorphic to $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_3)$ and to the unit group of the Hurwitz integral quaternions — a finite subgroup of $\mathrm{SU}(2) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Spin}(3)$ that appears in McKay-correspondence ADE classification as the $E_6$ node. **Spin-Galois cohomology**: extends the classical $\mathrm{Br}(\mathbb{Q}) = H^2(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}), \overline{\mathbb{Q}}^\times)$ Brauer group to *spin*-cohomology $H^2(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}), \mathrm{Spin}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n))$, governing whether projective Galois representations lift to linear ones. **What's open for Lean formalization**: Mathlib has scaffolding for $H_n(G, \mathbb{Z})$ (`Mathlib.RepresentationTheory.GroupCohomology.LowDegree`, `Mathlib.Algebra.Homology.HomotopyCategory`), but $H_2$ for specific finite groups like $A_n$ is not yet computed. Formalizing $H_2(A_n, \mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ for $n \geq 4$ (with the $H_2(A_6) = H_2(A_7) = \mathbb{Z}/6$ exceptional cases) would require: (i) Schur's *transgression* construction of the universal central extension via $1 \to M(G) \to \widetilde{G} \to G \to 1$ classified by the identity element of $H^2(G, M(G))$, (ii) explicit presentations of $\widetilde{A}_n$ by generators and relations (the *Schur generators* — preimages of double transpositions in $A_n$ satisfying $\tilde{t}_i^2 = z$ where $z$ generates the center, for $i = 1, \ldots, n-1$), (iii) the McKay-correspondence identification $\widetilde{A}_4 \cong \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_3)$, $\widetilde{A}_5 \cong \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_5)$ for the binary tetrahedral and binary icosahedral groups. Estimated effort: $\sim 1200$ LOC (the main bottleneck is Mathlib's nascent $H_2$ computations for non-abelian $G$), would give Mathlib its first machine-verified Schur multiplier computation for an infinite family of finite groups. **Why this complements this file's central lemma**: the simplicity of $A_5$ proved here pins the *quotient structure* of the alternating group (no non-trivial normal subgroups), while the Schur multiplier $H_2(A_5, \mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ pins the *central extension structure* (exactly one non-trivial double cover). Together they classify $A_n$ in its 'rigid neighborhood': $A_5$ has *one* projective representation type beyond the linear ones (the half-spin), and *zero* non-trivial normal subgroups — making $A_5$ simultaneously the smallest non-abelian simple group and the smallest non-trivially-spin-covered finite simple group. The McKay correspondence makes the connection explicit: $\widetilde{A}_5 \cong \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_5)$ of order 120 is the *binary icosahedral group*, the finite subgroup of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ corresponding to the affine Dynkin diagram $\widetilde{E}_8$ — the same $E_8$ Lie algebra that underlies the largest exceptional simple Lie group, completing the chain *$A_5$ simple $\to A_5 \cong I$ icosahedral $\to \widetilde{A}_5 = 2.I = \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_5) \to E_8$ exceptional Lie group*. The Schur multiplier $\mathbb{Z}/2$ is the universal-cover obstruction at every link in this chain — the file's simplicity lemma is the first link, but the spin-cohomological enrichment makes precise how that simplicity reverberates through algebraic Lie theory.

**Feit-Thompson odd order theorem (1963) and the Coq → Lean formalization frontier — the strict generalization of this file's classification**: This file proves $S_n$ (and $A_n$) is solvable iff $n \leq 4$, with $A_5$ at $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ as the smallest non-solvable group. The **Feit-Thompson theorem** (W. Feit and J. G. Thompson 1963, *Solvability of groups of odd order*, Pacific J. Math. 13: 775–1029, reference list above) is the strict structural generalization: *every finite group of odd order is solvable* — equivalently, every non-solvable finite group has even order, hence contains an involution by Cauchy's theorem. Chained with Burnside's $p^a q^b$ theorem (W. Burnside 1904, openQuestion #7), this gives the **sharp arithmetic lower bound** for non-solvability: every non-solvable finite group has order divisible by at least 3 distinct primes, with the smallest example being $|A_5| = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 = 60$ — *saturating* the Feit-Thompson-plus-Burnside lower bound. Thus this file's central protagonist $A_5$ is not merely *a* smallest non-solvable group but the *unique* smallest in the order-divisibility sense: any smaller order is either odd (forbidden by Feit-Thompson), or has at most 2 prime divisors (forbidden by Burnside), or is $\leq 24$ (where all groups are solvable by direct enumeration). **Historical scale**: the Feit-Thompson paper occupies 254 pages of a single journal issue and held the record as the longest single-theorem proof in mathematics until Gorenstein-Lyons-Solomon's CFSG (Classification of Finite Simple Groups, 2004, $\sim$15,000 pages across 30+ monographs). The proof's three-pillar structure — (i) **local analysis** classifying the centralizer structure of involutions and odd-order subgroups in a minimal counterexample, (ii) **character theory** using Frobenius's irreducibility framework (keyInsight #18) to constrain the dimensions of certain exceptional representations, (iii) **generators and relations** producing an explicit presentation contradicting odd order — is the archetypal blueprint for CFSG and the source of Thompson's 1970 Fields Medal. **The Coq formalization (Gonthier et al. 2012)**: G. Gonthier, A. Asperti, J. Avigad, Y. Bertot, C. Cohen, F. Garillot, S. Le Roux, A. Mahboubi, R. O'Connor, S. Ould Biha, I. Pasca, L. Rideau, A. Solovyev, E. Tassi, L. Théry — *A machine-checked proof of the odd order theorem*, ITP 2013 (LNCS 7998: 163–179) — completed at Inria Microsoft Research Joint Centre over $\sim$6 calendar years and $\sim$15 person-years of work, totaling approximately 170,000 lines of Coq code on top of the custom SSReflect tactic language and Mathematical Components library (which itself required years of development to support the proof). This was the **largest formal mathematics project of its era** and the first machine-verified proof of a major 20th-century theorem in pure algebra. The formalization revealed several minor gaps and ambiguities in the original Bender-Glauberman simplification (1994) but no errors in the substance of the Feit-Thompson argument — providing a high-confidence machine certificate for one of group theory's deepest results. **The Lean formalization frontier (2026)**: Mathlib has neither Feit-Thompson nor full Burnside $p^a q^b$ — current Mathlib (`Mathlib.GroupTheory.Solvable`, `Mathlib.GroupTheory.PGroup`) has $p$-groups solvable (Burnside's $p^a$ case via lower central series) but not $p^a q^b$. The natural Lean formalization staging, building on this file's `symmetric_solvable_iff`, is: (1) **Complete Burnside $p^a q^b$ in Lean** via the character-theoretic proof (cross-reference `abel-ruffini-galois-extensions-oq-07`) — currently the active formalization frontier, $\sim$2000 LOC building on Mathlib's nascent `RepresentationTheory.Character` infrastructure plus algebraic integers. (2) **Port Bender-Glauberman's CN-group / CIT-group lemmas** to Lean — Suzuki's classification of Zassenhaus groups (1962) and Bender's $p$-local analysis (1970, Annals of Mathematics 92: 33–47) furnish the local-structural inputs to Feit-Thompson, $\sim$5000 LOC translating from the Coq Mathematical Components formalization. (3) **Build exceptional character theory** — Brauer-Suzuki's exceptional character / coherence theory (1959, Illinois J. Math 3: 174–184) is the character-theoretic engine of Feit-Thompson, requiring Mathlib's representation theory to reach the level of *induced characters*, *Brauer's induction theorem*, and *p-modular representations* (currently absent from Mathlib 2026), estimated $\sim$8000 LOC. (4) **Complete the bulk of Feit-Thompson** combining (1)–(3) with the three-pillar structure of the original proof, $\sim$15,000–20,000 LOC depending on tactic-language sophistication — the Coq version's 170,000 LOC includes substantial general-purpose library scaffolding that Mathlib already provides, so the *Lean-specific* delta would be smaller. **Total estimated effort**: 10+ person-years for a coordinated community project, on the order of Mathlib's largest single-theorem formalizations to date (Liquid Tensor Experiment by Scholze-Commelin 2022 at $\sim$30,000 LOC, Polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa by Tao et al. 2023 at $\sim$30,000 LOC). **What completion would yield**: (a) Mathlib's first formal proof from the **CFSG-precursor tradition** Frobenius (1896) → Burnside (1904) → Brauer (1947) → Suzuki (1955) → **Feit-Thompson (1963)** → Aschbacher (1976) → CFSG (Gorenstein-Lyons-Solomon 2004) — making the full Frobenius-to-Feit-Thompson chain machine-verified in Lean, with this file's $A_5$-simplicity already established as the first link. (b) Direct corollary: every odd-order Galois group is solvable, so every odd-degree polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ whose splitting-field degree is odd is automatically *solvable by radicals* — sharpening Abel-Ruffini in the reverse direction (instead of 'degree $\geq 5$ might be unsolvable', odd degree with odd Galois group is *always* solvable). (c) Closure of openQuestion #7 (Burnside) as a sub-lemma of Feit-Thompson formalization, since the character-theoretic machinery developed for Feit-Thompson subsumes the $p^a q^b$ case. **Why this matters as the structural capstone**: this file proves the *first non-trivial* solvability classification ($S_n, A_n$ at the qualitative level); Feit-Thompson is the *strongest known general* solvability theorem applicable to *all* finite groups by their order alone. The two together bracket the discrete landscape of finite-group solvability: Feit-Thompson rules out odd-order non-solvability *globally*, and this file's classification exhibits the *smallest* non-solvable witness at order 60 — making $A_5$ at the *intersection* of the two theorems' sharp boundaries (smallest non-solvable; smallest even-order non-solvable; smallest non-solvable with three prime divisors). A Lean port of Feit-Thompson would give Mathlib its first machine-verified theorem whose statement is unconditional across the entire infinite family of finite groups — categorically stronger than this file's classification of specific families ($S_n, A_n$) — and would close the historical chain from Galois 1832 (first solvability classification, foreshadowing this file) through Burnside 1897 (first textbook synthesis) through Feit-Thompson 1963 (last great pre-CFSG monolithic theorem) at the level of *machine certification*. The estimated 10+ person-year cost reflects the proof's depth and the maturity required of Mathlib's representation-theoretic infrastructure — but the Coq precedent (Gonthier et al. 2012) establishes formalizability beyond doubt, making this an *engineering* rather than *mathematical* frontier.

additionalFiles.description: OQ-06 (S2): Primitive solvable permutation groups of prime degree p — Galois (1832) classification. Constructs the concrete affine group AGL(1, p) = ℤ/pℤ ⋊ (ℤ/pℤ)ˣ on (ZMod p) × (ZMod p)ˣ with the semidirect-product law `(a, u) * (b, v) = (a + u·b, u·v)`, supplies the manual `Group (AGL1Z p)` instance (associativity, identity, inverses), and proves the order calculation `Nat.card (AGL1Z p) = p · (p - 1)` via a bijection with the cartesian product (using `ZMod.card` and `ZMod.card_units_eq_totient` + `Nat.totient_prime`). Deferred to S3+: `IsSolvable (AGL1Z p)`, the natural permutation action `AGL1Z p →* Equiv.Perm (ZMod p)` and its primitivity, and the Galois direction embedding every primitive solvable subgroup of S_p into AGL(1, p).

mainTheorems.name: symmetric_solvable_iff
mainTheorems.description: Complete classification: the symmetric group $S_n$ is solvable if and only if $n \leq 4$. The forward direction discharges five cases by `interval_cases n <;> infer_instance` (delegating to the small-$n$ instances built in Part I); the reverse direction packages `symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le` via `by_contra; push_neg; omega`. This is the file's principal contribution to the gallery — the qualitative classification that, paired with Galois's solvability theorem (Mathlib `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`), yields Abel-Ruffini for the generic quintic.

mainTheorems.name: alternating_solvable_iff
mainTheorems.description: The alternating-group analogue: $A_n$ is solvable if and only if $n \leq 4$. The reverse direction follows by subgroup heredity from `symmetric_solvable_iff` ($A_n \leq S_n$); the forward direction goes through the sign-kernel exact sequence — were $A_n$ solvable for $n \geq 5$, then `solvable_of_ker_le_range` applied to the sign exact sequence would make $S_n$ solvable, contradicting the symmetric threshold. Combined with `symmetric_solvable_iff`, this pins the solvability boundary at $n = 4$ from both sides.

mainTheorems.name: a5_simple
mainTheorems.description: $A_5$ is a simple group (no non-trivial normal subgroups). The central obstruction underlying every non-solvability result in the file: $A_5$ simple and non-abelian forces it to appear as a non-cyclic composition factor in $S_n$ for all $n \geq 5$, blocking any abelian-factored composition series. Delegates to Mathlib's `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`, which internally runs the Sylow-counting argument detailed in keyInsight #8 ($n_2 = 5$, $n_3 = 10$, $n_5 = 6$, all $\neq 1$).

mainTheorems.name: not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_galois
mainTheorems.description: Contrapositive of Galois's solvability theorem: if the Galois group of a polynomial is not solvable, then no root is expressible by radicals. Composes Mathlib's `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` (forward direction of Galois's theorem) with negation via `intro hsol; exact hns (... hsol)` — a three-line proof bridging this file's group-theoretic classification (`symmetric_solvable_iff`, `a5_simple`) to the analytic statement of Abel-Ruffini. The named theorem makes the contrapositive directly citable in downstream proofs without unfolding the implication.
mainTheorems.leanType: {F E : Type*} [Field F] [Field E] [Algebra F E] {α : E} {q : F[X]} (hirr : Irreducible q) (hα : aeval α q = 0) (hns : ¬ IsSolvable (q.Gal)) : ¬ IsSolvableByRad F α

mainTheorems.name: sign_kernel_is_alternating
mainTheorems.description: The keystone identity $\ker(\mathrm{sgn} : S_n \to \{\pm 1\}) = A_n$ as a formal equality between subgroups. Proved by `ext` + `Equiv.Perm.mem_alternatingGroup`, this two-line theorem translates the abstract kernel of the sign homomorphism into the concrete alternating subtype and is the linchpin on which every short-exact-sequence argument in Part I pivots — used three times to lift solvability across $1 \to A_n \to S_n \to \mathbb{Z}^\times \to 1$ (for $n = 3, 4$) and $1 \to V_4 \to A_4 \to A_4/V_4 \to 1$.
mainTheorems.leanType: (n : ℕ) : (Equiv.Perm.sign : Equiv.Perm (Fin n) →* ℤˣ).ker = alternatingGroup (Fin n)

mainTheorems.name: galois_group_order
mainTheorems.description: The order of a finite Galois group equals the extension degree: $|\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)| = [E : F]$. Direct invocation of Mathlib's `IsGalois.card_aut_eq_finrank` under the standard hypotheses `[FiniteDimensional F E] [IsGalois F E]`. Establishes the numerical shadow of the Galois correspondence — the bijection between intermediate fields and subgroups in cardinality form — and provides the file's interface to extension degrees from downstream proofs that need to read off $|\mathrm{Gal}|$ from $[E:F]$.
mainTheorems.leanType: [FiniteDimensional F E] [IsGalois F E] : Nat.card (E ≃ₐ[F] E) = Module.finrank F E

mainTheorems.name: solvable_small_has_abelian_factors
mainTheorems.description: Joint solvability packaging for $n \leq 4$: simultaneously certifies $\mathrm{IsSolvable}(S_n)$ AND $\mathrm{IsSolvable}(A_n)$ as a single anonymous-constructor proof $\langle \text{symmetric\_solvable\_of\_le\_four } hn,\ \text{alternating\_solvable\_of\_le\_four } hn\rangle$. While `symmetric_solvable_iff` and `alternating_solvable_iff` give the full biconditional classifications, this paired conjunction is the form most directly consumed by downstream proofs that need *both* solvability witnesses to construct composition series with abelian factors (the canonical $\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_n \trianglelefteq S_n$ tower for $n \leq 4$, refined by $V_4$ at $n = 4$). Flagged as an original contribution in `meta.originalContributions[3]`: bundles two Mathlib instance inferences into a single ergonomic API surface without requiring re-derivation at the call site.
mainTheorems.leanType: (n : ℕ) (hn : n ≤ 4) : IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) ∧ IsSolvable (alternatingGroup (Fin n))

crossReferences.description: Abel-Ruffini impossibility theorem — this file adds the complete solvability classification of S_n, the group-theoretic engine underlying Abel-Ruffini

Sub-entry instantiating Mathlib's `JordanHolderLattice` typeclass for `Subgroup G` and deriving the Jordan-Hölder uniqueness theorem for groups. While this parent entry classifies which $S_n$ are solvable, `oq-04` deepens the analysis by proving that the composition series of $S_5$ ($\{e\} \triangleleft A_5 \triangleleft S_5$) is the *unique* such series — Jordan-Hölder guarantees no alternative decomposition avoids $A_5$. This uniqueness grounds the degree-5 threshold in structural necessity rather than one particular analysis. The sub-entry also surfaces the precise *gap* in Jordan-Hölder uniqueness: composition factors determine the group only up to *extension data* — an action $Q \to \mathrm{Aut}(N)$ together with a cohomology class in $H^2(Q, N)$ when $N$ is abelian (Schreier classification, Eilenberg-MacLane 1947). $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ vs $S_3$ illustrates: identical composition factors $\{\mathbb{Z}/2, \mathbb{Z}/3\}$ but distinguished by the trivial-vs-inversion action — making explicit that this parent entry's Jordan-Hölder uniqueness of $S_n$'s composition factor multiset does *not* alone explain why no alternative group exists with the same factors yet a different solvability status.

Shafarevich's Theorem (1954) — sub-entry formalizing the converse complement to this file's classification: every finite *solvable* group is realizable as $\text{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})$ for some Galois extension. Together with this parent's result ($S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$), Shafarevich completes the picture for the solvable side of the inverse Galois problem. The sub-entry axiomatizes the full theorem (proof requires class field theory + embedding problems beyond Mathlib) and derives 7 corollaries: cyclic groups, abelian groups, $S_3$, $S_4$ are all realizable; subgroups and quotients of solvable groups are realizable; $S_5$ is the first non-realizable-by-solvability example. A subsequent enrichment adds the *Burnside arithmetic criterion*: chaining Burnside's $p^a q^b$ theorem with Shafarevich yields a purely arithmetic test — every finite group whose order has at most two distinct prime factors is automatically Galois-realizable over $\mathbb{Q}$, with the bound sharp at $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ (the smallest order escaping the two-prime regime, and the smallest non-solvable group). This bridges this parent entry's openQuestion #5 (Shafarevich in Lean) and openQuestion #7 (Burnside in Lean) into a single computable-order criterion. Directly addresses this entry's openQuestion #5.

Shafarevich Feasibility in Mathlib — sub-sub-entry of `oq-05` answering the Lean-formalization side: how much of Shafarevich's theorem can be proved (rather than axiomatized) using Mathlib's developing class field theory? Answer: cyclic groups (proved via Dirichlet + Galois fixed fields in `InverseGalois.lean`) and coprime products (proved via CRT: $\mathbb{Z}/m \times \mathbb{Z}/n \cong \mathbb{Z}/(mn)$ when $\gcd(m,n)=1$) are fully provable today; general abelian groups require linear disjointness of cyclotomic subfields (~500 lines); full Shafarevich needs embedding problem theory (Brauer groups, Galois cohomology, Tate-Poitou duality) — not in Mathlib 2026. Together with `oq-05`, provides both the abstract statement and the Lean roadmap.

Burnside's $p^a q^b$ Theorem (Phase-2 Axiomatization) — sub-entry formalizing the structural converse referenced in this file's keyInsight #8 and openQuestion #7. Burnside (1904): every finite group of order $p^a \cdot q^b$ (at most two distinct primes) is solvable. The Phase-2 formalization proves the trivial cases axiom-free ($a=0$, $b=0$, $p=q$ reduce to `IsPGroup → IsNilpotent → IsSolvable`) and the squarefree-order case ($|G| = pq$, $p \neq q$ reduces to `IsZGroup.of_squarefree`); the genuinely-open non-trivial case is axiomatized as `burnside_pq_nontrivial`. The bound is sharp: $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ has *three* distinct primes — exactly the threshold this parent entry pins as the minimal non-solvable order. Chained with `oq-05`'s Shafarevich axiom (see that entry's *Burnside arithmetic criterion* keyInsight), Burnside also yields an automatic Galois-realizability test for every finite group of order $p^a q^b$ — bridging openQuestion #5 (Shafarevich) and openQuestion #7 (Burnside) into a single computable-order criterion. Partially addresses openQuestion #7.

Inverse Galois problem: while this file asks 'is S_n solvable?', the inverse Galois problem asks 'which groups occur as Galois groups?' The non-solvability of S₅ makes general quintics unsolvable, but the inverse Galois problem for S_n (every S_n occurs as a Galois group over ℚ) is also relevant

Both proofs use the same Galois theory machinery: this file proves S_n non-solvable for n ≥ 5 (blocking radical solutions), while angle-trisection-oq-02 proves the Galois group criterion for constructibility (2-group structure)
Lagrange's theorem |G| = |H| · [G:H] is used implicitly: the solvability chain S₄ ⊃ A₄ ⊃ V₄ ⊃ {e} has indices 2, 3, 4, and the tower law [S_n:ℤˣ] = |A_n| depends on Lagrange's theorem

Sylow theory provides the structural decomposition of groups used in solvability proofs. A group is solvable iff its Sylow subgroups satisfy certain conditions — the p-group components in the composition series are exactly the Sylow subgroups

Sylow-Based Simplicity Proof for $A_5$ — provides the explicit Sylow counting argument that this file invokes as a black-box from Mathlib's `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`. That entry computes $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$, the Sylow numbers $n_2 = 5$, $n_3 = 10$, $n_5 = 6$, shows no Sylow subgroup is normal, and uses the conjugacy class arithmetic $\{1, 12, 12, 15, 20\} = 60$ to rule out intermediate normal subgroups. Together: this file uses A₅ simplicity as the engine of non-solvability; the Sylow entry exhibits the underlying counting proof. This is the canonical 'why is $A_5$ simple?' demonstration referenced by Rotman §3.7 and Dummit-Foote §6.2.

Wiedijk #72 — the complete formalization of Sylow's three theorems (existence, conjugacy, and the counting constraint $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ with $n_p \mid [G:P]$). Foundational for $A_5$ simplicity that drives this file's non-solvability classification: applied to $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$, Sylow counting forces $n_2 = 5$, $n_3 = 10$, $n_5 = 6$ — all exceeding 1, so no Sylow subgroup is normal. Combined with conjugacy-class arithmetic this yields $A_5$ simple, which Mathlib's `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five` (invoked at `a5_simple`, lines 191–193 here) ultimately rests upon.

Orbit enumeration of Sylow $p$-subgroups: $n_p = [G : N_G(P)]$ via the orbit-stabilizer theorem. All Sylow $p$-subgroups form a single conjugation orbit $\{gPg^{-1} \mid g \in G\}$; the normality criterion $n_p = 1 \Leftrightarrow P \trianglelefteq G$ is the precise mechanism underlying $A_5$ simplicity. For $A_5$: $n_5 \mid 12$ and $n_5 \equiv 1 \pmod 5$ give $n_5 \in \{1, 6\}$; the criterion $n_5 = 1 \Rightarrow P_5 \trianglelefteq A_5$ contradicts simplicity, forcing $n_5 = 6$ — establishing the chain of reasoning that the `a5_simple` theorem black-boxes via Mathlib.

Constructs from scratch the Sylow-theoretic proof that $A_5$ (order $60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$) is simple: explicit computation of Sylow numbers $n_2 = 5$, $n_3 = 10$, $n_5 = 6$ by enumeration, demonstration that no Sylow subgroup is normal, and confirmation of simplicity via conjugacy-class analysis $\{1, 12, 12, 15, 20\} = 60$. This is the elementary first-principles version of the very black-box this file uses: `a5_simple` (lines 191–193) delegates to `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`, while `sylow-theorem-oq-04` provides the standalone Sylow-counting verification — together exposing the same mathematical fact at both library and foundational levels.
Abel-Ruffini proof chain: $A_5$ simple → $S_n$ not solvable for $n \geq 5$ — the step-by-step chain this file packages into the complete biconditional $S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$
S₂, S₃, S₄ solvability classification — a dedicated entry for the positive half of the biconditional, complementary to this file's complete classification including $n \geq 5$

Concrete Abel-Ruffini: proves $\text{Gal}(x^5 - 4x + 2) \cong S_5$ and derives unsolvability for this specific polynomial — the explicit instantiation of the non-solvability theorem this file formalizes for all $n \geq 5$

Alternating Groups: $A_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$ — the direct alternating-group analogue of this file's symmetric group classification, proved independently. This file's `alternating_solvable_iff` and that entry's main theorem are equivalent statements from complementary perspectives.

Finite Groups of Order $< 60$ Are Solvable — $|A_5| = 60$ is the precise boundary: every finite group of order $< 60$ is solvable. This entry proves the p-group chain $\text{IsPGroup} \Rightarrow \text{IsNilpotent} \Rightarrow \text{IsSolvable}$, establishing the order-60 threshold that makes $A_5$ the minimal non-solvable example.

Bring-Jerrard Reduction: any quintic can be transformed to the canonical form $x^5 + x + t = 0$ via Tschirnhaus substitutions. The resulting Bring radical $\mathrm{BR}(t)$ — the unique real root — provides a 'closed-form' solution to quintics, but one not expressible by radicals. This is fully consistent with this file's central result: $S_5$ not solvable means no radical tower can express roots of the reduced quintic for generic $t$. The Bring-Jerrard entry and this file together delimit the boundary between 'solvable' and 'transcendental' quintic solutions.

Galois's Solvability Criterion: a root is solvable by radicals $\iff$ its Galois group is solvable. This entry proves the forward direction from Mathlib and axiomatizes the reverse (Kummer theory). Complementary to this file's `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_galois` (contrapositive form) and the `galois_group_order` result.

Inverse Galois Problem: Non-Solvable Frontier — independently proves the same biconditionals ($S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$, $A_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$, $A_5$ simple) from the Inverse Galois Problem perspective. Where this file uses these results to explain quintic unsolvability (Abel-Ruffini), that entry uses them to delimit which groups can appear as Galois groups over $\mathbb{Q}$ — two complementary perspectives on the same structural boundary at $n = 4$.

A₅ Realizable over ℚ — the logical complement to this entry's non-solvability theorem. This file proves $A_5$ is the minimal obstruction (simple, non-solvable), while `inverse-galois-oq-06` constructs an explicit quintic $q(x) = x^5 - 5x^4 + 10x^3 - 10x^2 + 25x - 5$ with $\text{Gal}(q/\mathbb{Q}) \cong A_5$, proving $A_5$ is realizable. Together: the obstruction $A_5$ not only blocks radical solvability but also concretely occurs as the symmetry group of algebraic roots over $\mathbb{Q}$.

A₅ as a Galois Group over ℚ: The First Non-Solvable Realization — dedicated gallery entry for the same Lean file `Proofs/InverseGaloisA5.lean` (84 theorems, 1 axiom) that `inverse-galois-oq-06` also surfaces, with a sharper focus on *how* the realization is established. The two-stage Galois group identification is: (1) the **Vandermonde discriminant proof** that $\text{Gal}(q/\mathbb{Q}) \subseteq A_5$ — computing $\Delta(q) = \prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i - \alpha_j)^2$ as a square in $\mathbb{Q}$ forces the Galois action to preserve the sign-of-permutation, exactly the discriminant square test cited in this entry's keyInsight #10; (2) a single axiom `three_dvd_gal_card` (Dedekind's theorem on prime factorization of the discriminant: if a prime $p$ divides $\Delta(q)$ in a specific way, then $|\text{Gal}(q/\mathbb{Q})|$ has a $3$-cycle, forcing $3 \mid |\text{Gal}|$) which, combined with the upper bound $|\text{Gal}| \leq |A_5| = 60$ from stage (1), and lower bounds from irreducibility ($5 \mid |\text{Gal}|$) and transitivity, pins $|\text{Gal}| = 60$ exactly. The dual-pointer relationship is intentional: this parent entry establishes $A_5$ as the *abstract* obstruction; `inverse-galois-a5` exhibits it *concretely* as a Galois group; `inverse-galois-oq-06` packages the same realization as an open-question resolution within the inverse-Galois-problem framework. Together they form the canonical 'why is $A_5$ the boundary?' triple — abstract classification, concrete realization, and open-problem context.

Kronecker's Jugendtraum (Hilbert's 12th Problem) — the *next frontier* directly beyond this entry's conclusion implication #8. Implication #8 lays out the inverse-Galois trichotomy: (abelian over $\mathbb{Q}$ = Kronecker-Weber 1886, complete) $\subset$ (solvable over $\mathbb{Q}$ = Shafarevich 1954, complete) $\subset$ (arbitrary finite groups over $\mathbb{Q}$ = open since Hilbert 1892). Kronecker's *Jugendtraum* ('youth dream', voiced in a letter to Dedekind 1880) sharpens the *abelian* corner: not just to *prove* every abelian extension of an imaginary quadratic field $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$ exists (Takagi's class field theory 1920 does that), but to *exhibit explicit generators* for them — specifically, generators built from special values of analytic functions on a moduli space attached to $K$, generalizing the cyclotomic generators $\zeta_n$ that Kronecker-Weber uses for $K = \mathbb{Q}$. Hilbert promoted the dream to **Hilbert's 12th problem** in his 1900 ICM address: extend Kronecker-Weber from $\mathbb{Q}$ and imaginary quadratic fields to *all* number fields by finding analogous explicit analytic generators. **Status**: the imaginary-quadratic case was resolved by the **theory of complex multiplication** (Kronecker 1880s, Weber 1908, Hasse 1927, Shimura-Taniyama 1961) using elliptic modular functions and CM elliptic curves; the totally real case is conjecturally resolved by **Stark's conjectures** (Stark 1971–1980), still open in general; and **all other** number fields (e.g., $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})$) remain wide open in 2026, despite partial results from $p$-adic $L$-functions and Eisenstein cohomology. The connection to this entry's classification is *threefold*: (1) Hilbert's 12th is the *constructive* refinement of the abelian corner of the inverse Galois trichotomy referenced in implication #8 — settling 'which generators?' beyond Takagi's 'which subgroups?'; (2) the analytic functions appearing in the imaginary-quadratic case are exactly the *modular functions* that appear in Hermite's quintic-by-theta-constants solution (referenced in keyInsight #11) — both come from $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$-equivariant geometry, making Hilbert's 12 and Abel-Ruffini two faces of the same modular-function framework; (3) the icosahedral $A_5 \cong \mathrm{PSL}(2, 5)$ that this entry pins as the minimal non-solvable obstruction also appears in Hilbert's 12 as the *first* place where the abelian theory of complex multiplication fails to extend — at quintic CM number fields, the modular-function recipe for Hilbert's 12 collides with the non-solvability of $A_5$, requiring a fundamentally new construction. This makes Hilbert's 12 the natural continuation question for any reader of this entry: *given that $S_n$ is solvable iff $n \leq 4$, and given that every solvable group occurs as a Galois group (Shafarevich), can we exhibit those Galois extensions explicitly?*

Mathieu Group $M_{23}$ — the only sporadic simple group not yet known to be a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$. This entry classifies $S_n$ solvability via the smallest non-abelian simple group $A_5$; `inverse-galois-oq-02` explores the frontiers of the classification of finite simple groups (CFSG) by formalizing $M_{23}$: proving it is perfect ($[M_{23}, M_{23}] = M_{23}$), non-solvable, with $|M_{23}| = 2^7 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 23$, and not covered by Shafarevich's theorem (which applies only to solvable groups). Together, $A_5$ (the minimal non-solvable group, order 60) and $M_{23}$ (a sporadic non-solvable group, order 10,200,960) represent the two structural extremes of non-solvability that this file's classification theorem implicitly touches.

Cardano's cubic formula (Wiedijk #37, 1545) — the constructive realization of $S_3$'s solvability proved in this file. The composition series $\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_3 \trianglelefteq S_3$ with abelian factors $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$ and $S_3/A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ corresponds exactly to the two-layer radical tower in Cardano's formula: a square root (for the discriminant, $\mathbb{Z}/2$ layer) followed by a cube root (for the resolvent, $\mathbb{Z}/3$ layer). This file proves $S_3$ solvable via the short exact sequence $1 \to A_3 \to S_3 \to \mathbb{Z}^\times \to 1$ using `solvable_of_ker_le_range`; Cardano's formula is the algorithmic content of that exact sequence.

Ferrari's quartic formula (Wiedijk #100 candidate, 1540) — the constructive realization of $S_4$'s solvability proved in this file. General Dihedral-Galois Criterion for $X^n - a$ (Schinzel-Velez classification) — sub-entry of `inverse-galois-d4` that sharpens this file's solvable-side classification with a *parametric* characterization of which binomial radical extensions $X^n - a$ yield dihedral Galois groups. While this entry proves $S_n$ (and hence its dihedral subgroups $D_n \leq S_n$) is solvable for $n \leq 4$, the Schinzel-Velez theorem (Schinzel-Velez 1989, *J. The prerequisite Capelli irreducibility theorem (`Capelli's theorem`, classical 1898) is *absent* from Mathlib 4.26.0 — making this sub-entry's S2 axiomatization of the Schinzel-Velez characterization a precise marker of the *formalization frontier* for parametric dihedral Galois realizations. Casus Irreducibilis — concrete Lean formalization of keyInsight #15 (Isaacs 1985, $\mathbb{R}$-radical solvability iff Galois group is a 2-group). That sub-entry of `solution-of-cubic-oq-03` proves the *minimal* explicit witness of the Isaacs criterion: for the depressed cubic $x^3 + px + q = 0$, the casus irreducibilis is precisely when the discriminant $\Delta = -4p^3 - 27q^2 > 0$, which forces three distinct real roots yet requires Cardano's formula to take complex cube roots — an irreducible appearance of $\mathbb{C}$ inside a problem with entirely real roots. The Galois-theoretic explanation matches this file exactly: the splitting field $\mathrm{SF}(x^3 + px + q)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ has Galois group $S_3$ (generic) or $A_3$ (when $\Delta$ is a square in $\mathbb{Q}$); neither has order a power of $2$ ($|S_3| = 6 = 2 \cdot 3$, $|A_3| = 3$), so by Isaacs (1985) no $\mathbb{R}$-radical tower can express the roots even though they all lie in $\mathbb{R}$. The concrete witness in the sub-entry is $x^3 - 7x + 6 = (x-1)(x-2)(x+3)$ with $\Delta = -4(-7)^3 - 27 \cdot 6^2 = 1372 - 972 = 400 > 0$ — three rational roots, yet Cardano's formula necessarily passes through $\mathbb{C}$. This complements the file's $S_n$-solvable classification with a *finer* threshold within the solvable regime: at $n = 3$, the formula exists by radicals (this file's `S_3` solvability) but *not* by real radicals (Isaacs). The sub-entry also states Wantzel's impossibility theorem in this guise — sharpening the 'every cubic is solvable by radicals' content of this file's `S_3` case to 'every cubic is solvable by $\mathbb{C}$-radicals, but generic cubics with three real roots require an irreducible complex passage'. Together with this entry's keyInsight #15 reference to Isaacs, this provides the cluster's canonical bridge between the $\mathbb{Q}$-radical solvability of $S_3$ proved abstractly here and the constructive $\mathbb{R}$-vs-$\mathbb{C}$-radical distinction proved concretely in the casus irreducibilis sub-entry.

Chebotarev Density Theorem (1922) — provides the *statistical/density-theoretic* perspective complementing this file's qualitative solvability classification. While this entry proves $S_5$ non-solvable, Chebotarev quantifies the structure: in a Galois extension $L/\mathbb{Q}$ with $\text{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q}) = G$, primes distribute among Frobenius conjugacy classes with density $|C|/|G|$ for each class $C$. Applied to $S_5$: the 7 conjugacy classes (sizes 1, 10, 15, 20, 20, 24, 30 summing to 120) give the prime-splitting type distribution; for $A_5$: 5 conjugacy classes (sizes 1, 12, 12, 15, 20 — exactly the $\{1, 12, 12, 15, 20\}$ partition cited in this entry's keyInsight #8) determine the Chebotarev densities. Chebotarev thus provides a *statistical detection of solvability via prime density signatures*: the conjugacy-class structure forced by simplicity (no normal subgroups except $\{e\}$ and $G$) translates into observable prime-splitting fractions in $\mathbb{Z}_L$.

Hilbert's 13th Problem and the Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem (1956-57) — the continuous-function counterpart to this entry's algebraic obstruction. Hilbert asked whether the degree-7 equation $x^7 + ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + 1 = 0$ admits a closed-form solution using only *two-variable* continuous functions; Kolmogorov (1956) and Arnold (1957) answered yes for arbitrary continuous functions via the superposition representation $f(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \sum_{q=0}^{2n} \Phi_q\!\left(\sum_{p=1}^n \varphi_{q,p}(x_p)\right)$. The contrast with this file's result is structural: in the *continuous* category, every function of $n$ variables reduces to one-variable functions plus addition; in the *algebraic* (radical) category, the non-solvability of $S_n$ for $n \geq 5$ blocks any analogous reduction. Together the two results delineate exactly which categories of functions admit Hilbert-13-style superposition: continuous (yes, all $n$), algebraic-by-radicals (no for $n \geq 5$, exactly the threshold this file pins). The essential-dimension framework $\text{ed}(S_5) \geq 2$ of Buhler-Reichstein (1997), referenced in this entry's openQuestion #9, quantifies the algebraic obstruction: a generic quintic requires at least 2 algebraic parameters in any closed form, where Hilbert had hoped 1 might suffice.

Liouville's Theorem on Integration (1835) — the **differential-algebra analogue** of this entry's classical Abel-Ruffini classification, directly instantiating keyInsight #14's Picard-Vessiot bridge. That entry formalizes the algebraic core of Liouville's theorem that $\int e^{-x^2} dx$ has no elementary antiderivative: it proves no polynomial $p \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ satisfies the *Risch ODE* $p' - 2xp = 1$ by a degree-raising argument (the operator $L[p] = p' - 2xp$ raises polynomial degree by 1, so the constant $1$ is unreachable). The structural parallel with this file is exact: where the *algebraic* Galois group $S_n$ (with $A_5$ as the simple non-solvable composition factor) obstructs radical solvability of the general quintic, the *differential* Galois group $G \leq \mathrm{GL}_n(C)$ of a linear ODE (with simple non-solvable algebraic groups like $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$, or finite simple subgroups like the icosahedral $A_5 \hookrightarrow \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$) obstructs integrability by quadratures. The two impossibility theorems share the same Tannakian-categorical framework (Deligne 1990): a Galois extension is a finite-group fiber functor; a Picard-Vessiot extension is an algebraic-group fiber functor; both Abel-Ruffini and Liouville's integration theorem are special cases of the same simple-non-abelian obstruction principle in different Tannakian categories. The companion entry's polynomial degree-raising lemma is the differential-algebra analogue of $A_5$'s simplicity argument formalized here: a single structural impossibility that propagates to a global non-existence theorem (no radical formula for the quintic / no elementary antiderivative for $e^{-x^2}$).

Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions (1837) — supplies the analytic existence input to the cyclic-Galois realizability that the direct sub-entry `abel-ruffini-galois-extensions-oq-05-oq-01` uses to give an axiom-free partial-Shafarevich proof. To realize $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ as a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$, the construction picks a prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod n$ (Dirichlet guarantees infinitely many) and forms the unique index-$n$ subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times \cong \mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q})$ whose fixed field $L \subset \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$ has $\mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q}) \cong \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Companion to the Kronecker-Weber cross-reference (`kroneckers-jugendtraum`): Dirichlet supplies the *existence* of cyclotomic primes underlying the Kronecker-Weber classification (every abelian extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ is cyclotomic), and Kronecker-Weber tells you *which* cyclotomic fields. Enumeration of the five Platonic solids (Wiedijk #65) — the geometric realization of this entry's key obstruction. KeyInsight #6 records that $A_5 \cong \mathrm{PSL}(2,5) \cong I$, where $I$ is the group of 60 orientation-preserving rotational symmetries of the regular icosahedron (equivalently, of its dual the dodecahedron). The Platonic-solids entry proves there are exactly five such regular convex polyhedra, with the icosahedron and dodecahedron forming the unique pair whose rotation group is the non-abelian simple $A_5$ (the tetrahedron's group is $A_4$, the cube/octahedron's is $S_4$, both solvable). Thus the abstract solvability threshold proved here ($S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$, with $A_5$ as the minimal obstruction) has a strikingly visual face: among the five Platonic solids, the icosahedron/dodecahedron pair is *precisely* the boundary case whose symmetry group cannot be radical-decomposed. Felix Klein's *Vorlesungen über das Ikosaeder und die Auflösung der Gleichungen vom fünften Grade* (1884) made this connection foundational: Klein constructed an explicit *transcendental* solution of the general quintic via the icosahedral modular function $J(\tau)$ and showed that every quintic with rational coefficients has a Tschirnhaus reduction to *icosahedral form* $z^5 + 5az^2 + 5bz + c = 0$. The icosahedral solution lies entirely *outside* the radical category obstructed in this file — instantiating keyInsight #11 (Hermite's modular escape) at the geometric level. Together: this entry pins the algebraic threshold, `platonic-solids` enumerates the geometric carrier, and Klein's icosahedral theory bridges the two via the modular function ring whose Galois group is $A_5$.

Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (Gauss 1799, Wiedijk #2) — supplies the **existence** half of the existence/constructibility duality that this file's solvability threshold completes. FTA asserts that every non-constant $p \in \mathbb{C}[x]$ has a root, equivalently $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed; therefore the splitting field of any $f \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ sits inside $\mathbb{C}$ and the Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ acts on a non-empty finite set of roots. FTA is what makes the question 'are the roots expressible in radicals?' well-posed in the first place: without it, one cannot speak of *the* splitting field as a concrete subfield of $\mathbb{C}$. The Abel-Ruffini line of work then refines the existence statement into a sharp **constructibility** statement: roots of any polynomial exist (FTA), but for degree $\geq 5$ they generically cannot be written using $+, -, \times, \div, \sqrt[n]{\cdot}$ — the obstruction being exactly the non-solvability of $S_n$ proved here. This is one of the great pairs in the history of algebra: Gauss's 1799 doctoral thesis settles existence; Ruffini (1799/1813) and Abel (1824/1826) settle non-constructibility a quarter-century later. The mismatch — algebraically closed roots that nonetheless escape the radical hierarchy — is precisely what motivated Galois (1830-32) to invent group theory: existence is an *analytic* fact (FTA proofs invoke Rouché's theorem, winding numbers, or compactness), while constructibility is a *group-theoretic* fact (the Galois group's composition series). Subordinate connection: FTA underpins the cardinality identity $|\mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})| = [L:\mathbb{Q}]$ used throughout this file (separability + algebraic closure of $\mathbb{C}$ in characteristic $0$), and it is the existence input to the inverse Galois problem (`inverse-galois-a5`, `inverse-galois-d4`, `inverse-galois-f20` cross-references), which asks not just whether roots exist but whether *any prescribed finite group* arises as a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$ inside $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subset \mathbb{C}$. Wiedijk #2; fully formalized in Mathlib via the standard analytic argument (0 sorries, 0 axioms).

Vieta's formulas (François Viète, *De aequationum recognitione et emendatione*, posthumous 1615) — the **explicit mechanism** by which the Galois group of a polynomial embeds into $S_n$. For a monic $f(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n (x - \alpha_i) = x^n - e_1 x^{n-1} + e_2 x^{n-2} - \cdots + (-1)^n e_n \in F[x]$, Vieta's formulas identify the coefficients with the **elementary symmetric polynomials** $e_k = \sum_{i_1 < \cdots < i_k} \alpha_{i_1} \cdots \alpha_{i_k}$. The fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials (Gauss 1815, Mathlib: `MvPolynomial.symmetricSubalgebra`) then identifies the $S_n$-invariant subring with $F[e_1, \ldots, e_n]$: a polynomial in $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ is $S_n$-invariant iff it is expressible in $e_1, \ldots, e_n$. **This is precisely what forces $\mathrm{Gal}(f/F) \subseteq S_n$**: any field automorphism of the splitting field that fixes $F$ must permute the roots (since they satisfy $f$) and must fix the coefficients (since they lie in $F$) — and Vieta's identities are the equational evidence that the coefficient-fixing condition is *equivalent* to the symmetric-function condition. So the Galois group is constrained to act through permutations of $\{\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n\}$, giving the canonical injection $\mathrm{Gal}(f/F) \hookrightarrow S_n$ that this file's classification ($S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$) then completely characterizes. **Three concrete downstream consequences** rely on Vieta plus this file: (1) **Discriminant square test** (keyInsight #10): $\Delta(f) = \prod_{i<j} (\alpha_i - \alpha_j)^2$ is $S_n$-symmetric so equals a polynomial in the coefficients via Vieta (computable from $f$ alone), and $\sqrt{\Delta(f)} = \prod_{i<j} (\alpha_i - \alpha_j)$ flips sign under odd permutations, so $\mathrm{Gal}(f/F) \subseteq A_n \iff \Delta(f) \in F^{\times 2}$. (2) **Newton's identities** (Vieta's iterated form): the power sums $p_k = \sum \alpha_i^k$ are computable from $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ via $p_k = e_1 p_{k-1} - e_2 p_{k-2} + \cdots$, giving a finite recursive algorithm to compute $\sum \alpha_i^k$ from $f$'s coefficients without ever locating the roots — used in algorithmic Galois group identification (GAP, PARI/GP). (3) **Lagrange resolvent** (keyInsight #9): the resolvent $L_\sigma = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \zeta_n^k \alpha_{\sigma^k(1)}$ for a cyclic $\sigma$ has $L_\sigma^n$ expressible in the $e_k$'s by Vieta-plus-Galois averaging, giving Cardano's cubic ($n=3$) and Ferrari's quartic ($n=4$) — and failing to reduce further for $n=5$ exactly because of $A_5$'s simplicity proved here. **Mathlib formalization**: `Polynomial.coeff_eq_esymm_roots_of_card` ties polynomial coefficients to elementary symmetric polynomials in the roots; `Polynomial.discriminant` and the symmetric-polynomial fundamental theorem give the algorithmic computation of $\Delta(f)$. Vieta's formulas are thus the **bridge** between the coefficient-level data accessible to a computer ($f$'s coefficients) and the root-level data on which $\mathrm{Gal}(f)$ acts ($\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ in the splitting field) — without this bridge, the abstract solvability theorem proved here would have no computational handle on concrete polynomials.

Quartic Discriminant and Ferrari's Resolvent Cubic — the **algebraic mechanism** that powers this file's `s4_solvable` theorem (Part III, lines 143–152). The exact sequence $1 \to A_4 \to S_4 \to \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \to 1$ used here proves $S_4$ solvable via solvability of $A_4$ (which itself decomposes through the Klein four-group $V_4$, Part II, lines 105–141), but the *constructive* reason this decomposition succeeds is Ferrari's 1540 identity: any depressed quartic $y^4 + py^2 + qy + r = 0$ factors as $(y^2 + p/2 + m)^2 = (2m)\,y^2 - qy + (m^2 + mp + p^2/4 - r)$ for any $m$, and choosing $m$ to be a root of the **resolvent cubic** $8m^3 + 8pm^2 + (2p^2 - 8r)m - q^2 = 0$ makes the RHS a perfect square. The companion entry proves the sharp identity $\Delta(\text{resolvent cubic}) = 64 \cdot \Delta(\text{quartic})$ relating the discriminants — and this discriminant identity is the algebraic shadow of the group-theoretic short exact sequence $V_4 \hookrightarrow S_4 \twoheadrightarrow S_4/V_4 \cong S_3$: the resolvent cubic's Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(\text{resolvent}/\mathbb{Q}) \subseteq S_3$ is the image of the quartic's Galois group under $S_4 \to S_4/V_4$. Galois theory thus *predicts* Ferrari's reduction: because $V_4$ is normal in $S_4$ with abelian quotient $S_3$, solving the quartic reduces to solving the cubic, with the cubic-to-quartic reduction realized algebraically as the resolvent. The companion entry also proves the 16-term elementary-symmetric-polynomial expansion of $\Delta(\text{quartic})$ in terms of $e_1, \ldots, e_4$ (computable from coefficients via the `vietas-formulas` cross-reference), and the 6-term depressed-quartic formula after Tschirnhaus substitution $x \mapsto x - e_1/4$ — both with 0 sorries in Mathlib. Together: this file proves *that* $S_4$ is solvable (composition-series argument), `solution-of-cubic` and the companion provide the *explicit* radical formulas Ferrari (1540) gave, and `vietas-formulas-oq-03-oq-05` provides the **discriminant-level bridge** $\Delta(\text{resolvent}) = 64\,\Delta(\text{quartic})$ that certifies the algebraic reduction matches the group-theoretic short exact sequence.

Hall's Theorem (Philip Hall, 1928, *Proc. London Math. Soc.*) — the **strongest converse of Lagrange's theorem** that exists, and a **characterization of solvability itself** for finite groups. Lagrange's theorem (1771) says $|H|$ divides $|G|$ for every subgroup $H \leq G$; the converse — *given $d \mid |G|$, does a subgroup of order $d$ exist?* — fails in general (the standard counterexample is $A_4$ of order 12, which has no subgroup of order 6, demonstrated in this file's `arg-klein-four-a4` annotation by the V₄-quotient argument). Hall's theorem restores the converse in a sharply restricted form: in a **finite solvable** group $G$, for every **Hall divisor** $d$ of $|G|$ — meaning $d \mid |G|$ and $\gcd(d, |G|/d) = 1$ — a subgroup of order $d$ exists, and all such subgroups (called **Hall subgroups**) are conjugate. Critically, Hall proved the **biconditional**: a finite group $G$ is solvable *iff* it has a Hall subgroup for every Hall divisor of $|G|$. This biconditional is the deepest known converse to Lagrange and gives a **group-theoretic characterization of solvability** independent of derived series or composition-series language — the version of `IsSolvable` used throughout this file. **Two direct connections to this file**: (1) **Subgroup existence in the $n \leq 4$ regime**: Hall's theorem applied to $S_4$ (order 24 = $2^3 \cdot 3$) guarantees Hall subgroups for every coprime factorization, e.g., the Sylow-3 subgroup of order 3 (= $\langle (1\,2\,3) \rangle$, a Hall subgroup since $\gcd(3, 8) = 1$) is unique up to conjugation — matching the `s4_solvable` theorem here. (2) **Failure of Hall in the $n \geq 5$ regime**: $A_5$ (order 60 = $2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$) is the smallest non-abelian simple group and *fails* the Hall existence property — it has no subgroup of order 15 (= $3 \cdot 5$, a Hall divisor since $\gcd(15, 4) = 1$), because such a subgroup would be cyclic (by classification of groups of order 15) and would contain a normal Sylow-5 subgroup, contradicting $A_5$'s simplicity. So the Hall obstruction at $n = 5$ is the *same* obstruction as $A_5$-simplicity (this file's `arg-a5-simple` annotation) viewed through the subgroup-existence lens. The companion entry formalizes Hall's theorem in Lean: the cyclic case via `orderOf_pow'` and `IsCyclic.exists_generator`, the prime-power case via Cauchy's theorem, and axiomatizes the general solvable case with a full proof sketch. The **complementarity** is thus structural: this file *classifies which $S_n$ and $A_n$ are solvable* (the answer: $n \leq 4$); Hall's theorem provides the *equivalent subgroup-existence characterization* that makes solvability a positive structural property rather than a negative chain-condition.

Hermite-Lindemann theorem (Hermite 1873 for $e$; Lindemann 1882 for $e^\alpha$ with $\alpha \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \setminus \{0\}$; Wiedijk #56) — the **transcendence-theoretic companion** to this file's group-theoretic Abel-Ruffini classification, distinguished from the sibling cross-reference in `abel-ruffini` (PR #21486) by emphasizing the **structural-obstruction parallel** rather than the impossibility-statement parallel. The sibling entry frames the link as 'expressibility hierarchy' ($\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subsetneq \mathbb{C}$, with Abel-Ruffini blocking the first inclusion and Hermite-Lindemann witnessing the second). This file's complementary framing: **both theorems are the *finite-vs-infinite* faces of the same Tannakian-categorical phenomenon** referenced in this entry's keyInsight #14 (Picard-Vessiot theory). Where keyInsight #14 traces the algebraic-Galois ↔ differential-Galois ↔ Tannakian-Galois ladder for the **solvability** classification proved here ($S_n$ solvable iff $n \leq 4$, via derived-series obstruction in finite group theory), Hermite-Lindemann sits at the **transcendence-theoretic** rung of the same ladder via its modern reformulation: **Lindemann-Weierstrass** ($e^{\alpha_1}, \ldots, e^{\alpha_n}$ algebraically independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ when $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ are $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent algebraic) is the **prototype theorem in motivic Galois theory** (Grothendieck's *motivic Galois group* and the *period conjecture* — Kontsevich-Zagier 2001, *Periods*, in Engquist-Schmid eds.). The structural parallel is precise: where this file's $A_5$-simplicity blocks the derived-series obstruction at depth $\geq 1$ in finite group theory (no abelian-factor composition series for $S_5$), the **motivic Galois group** $G_{\text{mot}}$ associated with the period algebra blocks an analogous derived-series obstruction at the level of mixed Tate motives — making $e, \pi$ transcendental for the same *Tannakian* reason that $S_5$ is non-solvable: both are obstructions in the derived/commutator structure of their respective Galois groups. **Two concrete payoffs of the analogy**: (1) **Lindemann-Weierstrass as 'transcendence Abel-Ruffini'**: just as this file's `symmetric_solvable_iff` certifies that no radical formula expresses the generic quintic's roots in terms of its coefficients, Lindemann-Weierstrass certifies that no algebraic relation expresses $e^{\alpha}$ in terms of $\alpha$ — the structural obstruction in both cases is the simplicity/non-abelian-quotient of an associated Galois-theoretic object ($A_5 \trianglelefteq S_5$ here; the unipotent radical of the motivic Galois group of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(e^{\alpha_1}, \ldots, e^{\alpha_n})$ for Lindemann-Weierstrass). (2) **The Schanuel conjecture as the universal upper bound**: Schanuel's conjecture (1960s, unpublished — the master conjecture of transcendence theory, implying Lindemann-Weierstrass, Gelfond-Schneider, and the algebraic independence of $e, \pi$ over $\mathbb{Q}$) is the *transcendence-theoretic analog* of the inverse Galois problem (cross-reference `inverse-galois`): both ask which Galois-theoretic structures can be realized — finite Galois groups over $\mathbb{Q}$ in the inverse Galois case, motivic Galois groups of period algebras in the Schanuel case. The **Mathlib formalization frontier**: Hermite-Lindemann is formalized at `hermite-lindemann` (1 axiom, the theorem itself), the **derived corollaries** $e$ and $\pi$ transcendence (Wiedijk #67 and #53), and 4 additional consequences — paralleling this file's *0-axiom* solvability classification as the *finite/discrete* side of the Tannakian ladder, with Hermite-Lindemann's 1-axiom statement marking the *current* formalization boundary on the *infinite/transcendental* side. Joint formalization status (2026): both theorems are in Mathlib-adjacent gallery entries with sharp axiom-counts (this file: 0 axioms; `hermite-lindemann`: 1 axiom), making the Galois ↔ Lindemann-Weierstrass bridge the **shortest existing path** from finite-group derived-series obstructions to motivic-Galois transcendence obstructions in a fully machine-verifiable form.

Ferrari's resolvent cubic — the **constructive face** of this file's $S_4$ solvability classification. Where this file proves *qualitatively* that $S_4$ is solvable via the composition series $\{e\} \trianglelefteq V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$ with abelian factors $V_4, A_4/V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3, S_4/A_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ (theorem `s4_solvable`, lines 143–152, annotation `arg-s4-solvable`), this companion entry executes the *constructive recipe* that the qualitative classification predicts: Ferrari (1545, published in Cardano's *Ars Magna*) reduces the general quartic $x^4 + px^2 + qx + r = 0$ to a depressed cubic in an auxiliary variable $y$, whose Cardano-formula roots then yield the quartic's roots via two further square-root extractions. The chain of solvable extensions $\mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D_3}) \subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D_3}, \sqrt[3]{\cdot}) \subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D_3}, \sqrt[3]{\cdot}, \sqrt{\cdot}) \subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D_3}, \sqrt[3]{\cdot}, \sqrt{\cdot}, \sqrt{\cdot})$ is **exactly the radical tower** dual to the composition series proved here — a textbook instance of the Galois correspondence between subfield chains and subgroup chains (cross-reference `inverse-galois` for the chain-by-chain dictionary). The companion entry's chained Cardano formula thus provides the *witness* that the abelian-factor composition series predicted by this file's `s4_solvable` is actually realizable by radicals over $\mathbb{Q}$ — closing the loop: $S_4$ solvable (this file, group-theoretic) $\iff$ quartic solvable by radicals (companion, field-theoretic) $\iff$ Ferrari's chain exists (companion, constructive). This circular equivalence collapses at $n = 5$ — this file's $A_5$-simplicity (theorem `a5_simple`, lines 185–199, annotation `arg-a5-simple`) blocks the composition-series construction at $A_5$ for $S_5$, hence by Galois correspondence blocks any radical tower for the generic quintic, with **no analogous resolvent-quintic recipe possible** as Bring-Jerrard's 1786/1834 normal-form reduction (keyInsight #22) reaches only the *one-parameter* form $x^5 + x + a$ and cannot eliminate the remaining parameter $a$ by *radical* operations — exactly the obstruction this file's `symmetric_solvable_iff` certifies in qualitative form.

Discriminant of the depressed cubic $\Delta = -4p^3 - 27q^2 = \prod_{i<j}(x_i - x_j)^2$ — the **computational face** of keyInsight #10 (discriminant square test for $A_n$ vs $S_n$). This entry asserts at the *general* level that for an irreducible separable polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$ of degree $n$ with roots $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ in a splitting field, the **discriminant square root** $\delta = \prod_{i<j}(x_i - x_j)$ is a Galois-invariant under $A_n$ but flips sign under any odd permutation — hence $\mathrm{Gal}(f) \subseteq A_n \iff \delta \in \mathbb{Q} \iff \mathrm{disc}(f) = \delta^2$ *is a rational square*. The companion entry proves the $n = 3$ instance: $\Delta = -4p^3 - 27q^2$ is exactly $\delta^2$ for the three Cardano roots of $x^3 + px + q = 0$, making the discriminant-square test directly computable in degree 3 — when $\Delta$ is a perfect rational square, $\mathrm{Gal}(f) \subseteq A_3 = \mathbb{Z}/3$ (Galois group is cyclic of order 3); when $\Delta$ is *not* a square, $\mathrm{Gal}(f) = S_3$. **This is precisely the test that distinguishes $S_3$-Galois cubics from $A_3$-Galois cubics**, and the companion entry's identity $\Delta = (x_1-x_2)^2 (x_1-x_3)^2 (x_2-x_3)^2$ provides the *Vandermonde realization* of $\delta$ that the abstract test refers to. The generalization to higher $n$: $\mathrm{disc}(x^n + ax + b) = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(n^n b^{n-1} + (-(n-1))^{n-1} a^n)$ for the **trinomial** $x^n + ax + b$ (Selmer 1956 for $n = 5$ specifically, generalized in Cohen *A Course in Computational Algebraic Number Theory* §6.3), enabling the $A_n$ vs $S_n$ check that drives Stauduhar's algorithm (keyInsight #17) and the LMFDB tabulation. For the file's sample quintic $x^5 - 4x + 2$ (companion entry `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01`), $\mathrm{disc} = 5^5 \cdot 2^4 + (-4)^4 \cdot (-4)^5 = -2^{12} \cdot 47$, a non-square in $\mathbb{Q}$, certifying $\mathrm{Gal}(x^5 - 4x + 2) \not\subseteq A_5$, hence $\mathrm{Gal} = S_5$ when combined with $|\mathrm{Gal}| \geq 60$ from the splitting-field degree — exhibiting the discriminant test's *operational sharpness* even at the non-solvable threshold this file proves.

Vieta's formulas for the **general** cubic $x^3 + ax^2 + bx + c = (x-r_1)(x-r_2)(x-r_3)$ over any commutative ring — the **purely algebraic** statement of the symmetric-polynomial identities $a = -e_1$, $b = e_2$, $c = -e_3$ that this file's $S_3$-solvability proof implicitly relies on. The expansion $(x-r_1)(x-r_2)(x-r_3) = x^3 - (r_1+r_2+r_3)x^2 + (r_1 r_2 + r_1 r_3 + r_2 r_3)x - r_1 r_2 r_3$ is the **coefficient–root duality** that makes the Galois group act as permutations on roots while fixing coefficients — the foundational fact that *the action of $\mathrm{Gal}(f/\mathbb{Q})$ permutes roots and fixes elementary symmetric functions of those roots* underwrites every Galois-theoretic argument in this file, including the small-$n$ solvability constructions (Parts I–II) and the $n \geq 5$ obstruction (Parts III–V). The ring-generic formulation (proved over any `CommRing`, not just $\mathbb{C}$ or $\mathbb{Q}$) emphasizes that Vieta's identities are an **algebraic theorem about polynomial expansion**, not an analytic statement about complex roots — the same identities hold over $\mathbb{F}_p$ (where they drive the cubic formula characteristic-3 caveats), over $\mathbb{Z}$ (where they give integer-root bounds via the rational root theorem), and over function fields (where they underpin the resolvent constructions). This *separation of the algebraic content from the analytic content* is what allows the Galois correspondence to lift from $\mathbb{Q}$ to arbitrary base fields — the foundational layer beneath both the concrete Cardano-root verification (`solution-of-cubic-oq-03`) and the abstract $S_3 \to \mathbb{Z}^\times$ exact sequence used in this file's `perm_fin_3_solvable` instance (line 89).

**Liouville's 1844 construction of explicit transcendentals — the next rung of the expressibility hierarchy above Abel-Ruffini's algebraic-radical impossibility.** This file proves that $S_n$ ($n \geq 5$) is non-solvable, hence — via Galois's bridge — the roots of generic degree-$\geq 5$ polynomials over $\mathbb{Q}$ cannot be written using $\{+, -, \times, \div, \sqrt[k]{\,}\}$. Liouville (*Sur des classes très-étendues de quantités dont la valeur n'est ni algébrique, ni même réductible à des irrationnelles algébriques*, J. Math. Pures Appl. 16 (1851) 133–142, building on his 1844 *Comptes Rendus* announcement) exhibited the next layer: the *Liouville numbers* $\sum_{k=1}^\infty 10^{-k!}$ are real numbers that escape *all* polynomial equations with rational coefficients — they are transcendental, not algebraic of any degree. The mechanism is Diophantine: for every algebraic $\alpha$ of degree $n$, there exists $C > 0$ such that $|\alpha - p/q| > C/q^n$ for all $p/q \in \mathbb{Q}$ (Liouville's inequality), and Liouville's $\sum 10^{-k!}$ violates this bound for *every* $n$ by the super-fast factorial growth of the denominators. Where Abel-Ruffini (this file at $n \geq 5$) blocks $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ — algebraic numbers not expressible by radicals — Liouville blocks $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subsetneq \mathbb{R}$ — real numbers not algebraic at all. The combined hierarchy $\mathbb{Q} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subsetneq \mathbb{R}$ has *this file's threshold $n = 4$* as the precise location of the first non-trivial inclusion (algebraic-not-radical), and Liouville-1844 as the next strict inclusion (algebraic-not-real). Both are *expressibility impossibility theorems*: both translate a syntactic question (expressible by radicals; algebraic of any degree) into a structural invariant (solvable Galois group; Diophantine-approximation rate) whose absence witnesses impossibility. The methodological parallel — pioneered by Wantzel 1837 generalizing Abel-Ruffini's template (cross-reference `angle-trisection-oq-02`) — is exact: identify a class invariant, characterize the expressible class, exhibit a violator. The gallery's `liouville-theorem` formalizes the constructive transcendental side of this hierarchy with 16 theorems, 0 axioms, 0 sorries, placing this file's negative-algebraic side and Liouville's negative-transcendental side on the same Lean-verified arc.

**Cantor 1874: the algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ is countable — the cardinality face of the same expressibility hierarchy this file's classification populates.** This file proves the $S_n$ solvability dichotomy $n \leq 4$ vs $n \geq 5$ that pinpoints which algebraic numbers are radically expressible. Cantor's 1874 theorem (*Über eine Eigenschaft des Inbegriffs aller reellen algebraischen Zahlen*, Crelle 77: 258–262) supplies the *cardinality* counterpart: $|\overline{\mathbb{Q}}| = \aleph_0$, because $\mathbb{Q}[X] = \bigcup_n \mathbb{Q}[X]_{\deg \leq n}$ is a countable union of countable sets and each polynomial has only finitely many roots. **The triple cardinality–expressibility–Galois picture**: $|\mathbb{Q}| = |\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}}| = |\overline{\mathbb{Q}}| = \aleph_0 < 2^{\aleph_0} = |\mathbb{R}|$. Even though the cardinalities of the three algebraic strata coincide, the inclusions $\mathbb{Q} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ are *strict*, and strictness is witnessed exactly by the structures this file classifies: solvable $S_n$ ($n \leq 4$) realizes elements of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}}$ via Cardano/Ferrari radical formulas; non-solvable $S_n$ ($n \geq 5$) realizes elements of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} \setminus \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}}$ via Galois-group obstruction. The cardinality gap $\aleph_0 < 2^{\aleph_0}$ then gives — Cantor's deeper 1874 contribution — the existence of transcendentals as a measure-theoretic consequence ($|\mathbb{R} \setminus \overline{\mathbb{Q}}| = 2^{\aleph_0}$, hence non-empty, with the algebraic numbers a Lebesgue-null set inside $\mathbb{R}$). The gallery `algebraic-numbers-countable` formalizes Cantor's countability theorem; this entry's $S_n$ classification formalizes the algebraic-radical sub-stratum classification — together they verify the full algebraic-numbers picture: a countable, completely classified, but radically-non-expressible-from-degree-5-onward subfield of $\mathbb{R}$. Methodologically the two formalizations exhibit the same expressibility-impossibility pattern (cf. Wantzel 1837's generalization of Abel-Ruffini's template, cross-reference `angle-trisection-oq-02`) from two different angles: structural (Galois groups, this file) and cardinality-and-construction (countability + Cantor diagonal, `algebraic-numbers-countable`).

**Wilson's theorem $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod p$ — the combinatorial-number-theoretic identity behind the symmetric group order $|S_p| = p!$ that this file's solvability classification dissects.** Wilson's theorem (Edward Waring 1770 attribution, Lagrange 1771 first proof, gallery Wiedijk #57) characterizes primes via the factorial $p$ that *also* gives $|S_p| = p! = p \cdot (p-1)!$ — Lagrange's theorem in $S_p$. The connection runs through three structural layers: (i) **Cauchy's theorem and Sylow $p$-subgroups in $S_p$**: by Cauchy, $S_p$ contains an element of order $p$ for any prime $p$ — exactly a $p$-cycle, generating a Sylow $p$-subgroup $\langle\sigma\rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}/p$ of order $p$ inside $|S_p| = p!$. The number of Sylow $p$-subgroups is $n_p = (p-2)!$ by an orbit-stabilizer argument (each $p$-cycle has $p$ powers; the $(p-1)!/p$ cycles give $(p-2)!$ distinct Sylow $p$-subgroups, modulo $p$ via Sylow III gives $(p-2)! \equiv 1 \pmod p$, i.e., $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod p$ via $(p-1)(p-2)! \equiv -1 \cdot 1 = -1 \pmod p$). **Wilson's theorem is therefore Sylow III applied to $S_p$.** (ii) **Connection to this file's $p = 5$ classification**: for $p = 5$, Wilson gives $4! = 24 \equiv -1 \pmod 5$, equivalently $|A_5| = 60 = 5 \cdot 12$ with $12 = 4!/2$ being the number of 5-cycles per $A_5$-conjugacy class (cf. keyInsight on $A_5$ conjugacy classes $\{1, 15, 20, 12, 12\}$ in `abel-ruffini`). The Wilson identity $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod p$ is therefore the *combinatorial substrate* of the $A_5$-conjugacy-class arithmetic that powers the simplicity proof of $A_5$ used in this file's `alternating_solvable_iff` and ultimately `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_galois`. (iii) **Galois-theoretic reformulation via Lucas-Carmichael**: the **Lucas' theorem on multinomial coefficients** $(a + b)^p \equiv a^p + b^p \pmod p$ (the Freshman's Dream) and **Fermat's little theorem** $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ (for $\gcd(a, p) = 1$) are Wilson's algebraic siblings — all three reduce to the cyclotomic identity $\prod_{k=1}^{p-1} (X - \zeta_p^k) = X^{p-1} + X^{p-2} + \cdots + 1 = \Phi_p(X)$ evaluated at $X = 1$, giving $\prod_{k=1}^{p-1} (1 - \zeta_p^k) = p$ and (via the Galois conjugate at $X = 0$) $\prod_{k=1}^{p-1} (-\zeta_p^k) = (-1)^{p-1}$, which combines with $\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \zeta_p^k = -1$ to recover $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod p$. The deeper structural perspective: Wilson is the Galois-cohomological statement $H^1(\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q}), \mathbb{Z}/p) = 0$ for $p$ prime, the first non-trivial instance of Hilbert 90 in cyclotomic form. The gallery formalizes Wilson with 24 theorems, 0 axioms, 0 sorries, providing the Sylow-substrate result that backs this file's $|S_p|$ factorial counting and the conjugacy-class arithmetic underlying $A_5$'s simplicity. **Practical relevance to this file's keyInsights**: any explicit enumeration of $|S_n|$ orders that this file's Part XIV theorems (`card_s7 : |S_7| = 5040`, `card_s8 : |S_8| = 40320`, `card_a7 : |A_7| = 2520`, `card_a8 : |A_8| = 20160`) computes via `native_decide` is structurally a consequence of the Wilson-Lucas-Fermat triple — the factorial growth $|S_n| = n!$ that crosses the kernel-evaluator threshold of 360 at $n = 6$ is governed by exactly the prime-divisibility patterns Wilson's theorem captures.

references.title: Teoria generale delle equazioni, in cui si dimostra impossibile la soluzione algebraica delle equazioni generali di grado superiore al quarto
references.venue: Stamperia di S. Tommaso d'Aquino, Bologna (2 vols., 509 + 211 pp.)
references.note: Ruffini's first attempted proof of the unsolvability of the general quintic by radicals — predating Abel's rigorous proof by 25 years. Ruffini introduced what would later be called *permutation group* arguments (he used the term 'permutazione') to analyze how the roots of a quintic transform under the substitutions appearing in any hypothetical radical formula. The 1799 *Teoria generale* contained a gap (Ruffini implicitly assumed any algebraic function of the roots, when expressed in radicals, is itself expressible using the same radicals — the so-called *Ruffini-Abel theorem on natural irrationalities*), which Ruffini partially closed in subsequent revisions (1802, 1806, 1813) responding to criticism from Malfatti and others. The complete and rigorous resolution came with Abel (1824, next reference), who supplied the missing natural-irrationalities lemma and produced the modern unsolvability proof. Cauchy (1815) credited Ruffini in his foundational paper on permutation groups, calling Ruffini's argument 'incontestable' for the most important cases. Cited in the historicalContext as the *namesake* of the Abel-Ruffini theorem — Ruffini's name in the modern theorem name acknowledges his priority in identifying the group-theoretic obstruction, even though the rigorous proof is Abel's. See L. Toti Rigatelli, *Evariste Galois* (Birkhäuser 1996, §1.3) and R. Ayoub, 'Paolo Ruffini's contributions to the quintic' (Archive for History of Exact Sciences 23(3): 253-277, 1980) for the historical reconstruction of Ruffini's argument and its gap.

references.note: Foundational work introducing the Lagrange resolvent $L_\sigma = \sum \zeta^k \alpha_{\sigma^k(1)}$ and the systematic study of how permutation symmetries of the roots constrain solvability by radicals. Lagrange showed that Cardano's cubic and Ferrari's quartic formulas both arise from the same resolvent recipe, and noted that the analogous resolvent for the quintic factors through a sextic — implicitly anticipating Abel-Ruffini by half a century. Galois (1832) replaced Lagrange's resolvent calculus with the abstract theory of automorphism groups, but Lagrange's recipe remains the explicit algorithmic content of solvability proofs for $n \leq 4$. Cited in keyInsights #9.

references.note: Dedekind's lemma on linear independence of characters: distinct field homomorphisms $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_m : E \to L$ are linearly independent over $L$. This is the source of the inequality $|\text{Aut}(E/F)| \leq [E:F]$ for any finite extension — the Galois condition turns this inequality into equality. references.title: On the distribution of Galois groups
references.note: Malle's conjecture predicting the asymptotic count of number-field extensions $K/\mathbb{Q}$ of bounded discriminant with prescribed Galois group $G \leq S_n$. Refined in Malle (2004), 'On the distribution of Galois groups, II', Experimental Mathematics 13(2): 129–135. Known for $G$ abelian (Wright 1989), $S_3$ (Davenport-Heilbronn 1971), $S_4, S_5$ (Bhargava 2005, 2010); open for non-solvable $G$ including $A_5$. references.title: On functions of three variables
references.note: Arnold's resolution of Hilbert's 13th problem for continuous functions: every continuous function of three variables is a finite superposition of continuous functions of two variables, building on Kolmogorov's 1956 representation theorem. Combined with the algebraic obstruction proved here ($S_n$ not solvable for $n \geq 5$), this delineates a sharp boundary: the topological/continuous version of Hilbert's 13 succeeds, but the algebraic version fails — both governed by the symmetry obstructions of $S_n$. Cited in the openQuestion on essential dimension.

references.title: On the essential dimension of a finite group
references.note: Introduces the essential dimension $\text{ed}(G)$ of a finite group: the minimum number of algebraic parameters needed to define a generic Galois extension with Galois group $G$. Proves $\text{ed}(S_5) \geq 2$ — quantifying Abel-Ruffini: the general quintic with Galois group $S_5$ requires at least 2 algebraic parameters in any closed-form solution. The essential dimension is now a central invariant in algebraic geometry and Galois cohomology. Cited in the openQuestion on Hilbert's 13th problem.

references.title: Solvability of Groups of Odd Order
references.note: Every finite group of odd order is solvable — directly constrains the classification: A₅ (order 60, even) is the smallest non-solvable group, consistent with Feit-Thompson since all odd-order groups are solvable.
