references.note: Burnside's theorem: every finite group whose order has at most two distinct prime factors is solvable. This sharply complements the threshold proved here: $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ has *three* distinct primes — exactly one more than Burnside's bound — explaining why $A_5$ is the minimal non-solvable group. The original proof uses character theory (representation theory in characteristic 0); a character-free proof was given by Goldschmidt (1970) and Matsuyama (1973) using the focal subgroup theorem. Directly grounds the openQuestion on formalizing Burnside in Lean.

references.title: A group theoretic proof of the $p^\alpha q^\beta$ theorem for odd primes
references.note: Character-free proof of Burnside's theorem for the case where both primes are odd. Together with Matsuyama (1973) — who handled the case $p = 2$ — provides a fully elementary route to Burnside's $p^a q^b$ theorem, sidestepping representation theory. Cited in the openQuestion as the technical path most amenable to Lean formalization, since Mathlib has stronger group-theoretic infrastructure than character-theoretic infrastructure.

references.title: Traité des substitutions et des équations algébriques
references.note: The first systematic treatise on group theory and its application to polynomial equations. Jordan's *Traité* organized Galois's posthumously published manuscripts (Liouville 1846) into a coherent algebraic theory, introducing the modern terminology of *groupe* (group), *substitution* (permutation), *transitivité* (transitivity), and *primitivité* (primitivity) used throughout this Lean formalization (`Equiv.Perm`, transitive action, simple group). Book III ('Des équations algébriques') develops the complete solvability classification: $S_n$ solvable iff $n \leq 4$ via explicit derivation of the chain $\{e\} \trianglelefteq V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4 \trianglelefteq S_5$, with $V_4$ identified as 'le groupe quaternaire' (Jordan's name for the Klein four-group three years before Klein himself studied it). The *Traité* established that the simple group $A_5$ is the structural obstruction at $n = 5$, anticipating Hölder's 1889 formulation of the Jordan-Hölder theorem. Foundational reference for the entire solvability framework formalized in this file.

references.title: The density of discriminants of quartic rings and fields
references.note: Established Malle's conjecture for $G = S_4$: the number of quartic number fields $K/\mathbb{Q}$ with $|\text{disc}(K)| \leq X$ is asymptotically $c \cdot X$, with explicit constant $c$. Companion paper 'The density of discriminants of quintic rings and fields' (Annals of Mathematics 172(3): 1559–1591, 2010) proves the corresponding asymptotic for $G = S_5$. Together with Davenport-Heilbronn (1971) for $S_3$ and Wright (1989) for abelian groups, this fully resolves Malle's conjecture for $S_n$ with $n \leq 5$ via Bhargava's prehomogeneous-vector-spaces method (the basis of his 2014 Fields Medal). For $G = A_5$ (non-solvable, order 60), only the upper bound from Bhargava-Shankar-Tsimerman (2010) is known — the precise asymptotic remains open, the quantitative frontier directly beyond this file's qualitative threshold. Cited in the Malle-conjecture openQuestion.

references.title: Sur la résolution de l'équation du cinquième degré
references.venue: Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, Paris 46: 508–515
references.note: First explicit transcendental solution of the general quintic. After Bring-Jerrard reduction to the one-parameter form $x^5 - x + t = 0$, Hermite expressed the five roots as rational functions of theta constants $\vartheta_i(\tau)$ evaluated at five values of $\tau \in \mathbb{H}$ in a $\Gamma(5)$-orbit, where $\Gamma(5) \leq \mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{Z})$ is the principal congruence subgroup of level 5. The structural reason is the isomorphism $\mathrm{PSL}(2, \mathbb{Z})/\Gamma(5) \cong A_5 \cong I$ (icosahedral rotation group): the modular curve $X(5) = \overline{\mathbb{H}/\Gamma(5)}$ has automorphism group $A_5$ and provides the natural geometric setting for the five-root $A_5$-orbit. Hermite's paper appeared 26 years before Klein's *Vorlesungen über das Ikosaeder* (1884), which systematized the icosahedral-form approach. Together with Kronecker's independent 1858 solution and Brioschi's 1858 work, Hermite established that *the general quintic is solvable in modular functions* — sharpening Abel-Ruffini's negative result to a precise statement about which function class is required. Cited in keyInsight #11.

references.title: Meletemata quaedam mathematica circa transformationem aequationum algebraicarum
references.note: Erland Samuel Bring's 1786 doctoral dissertation establishing the **Bring reduction**: any general quintic $x^5 + a_4 x^4 + \cdots + a_1 x + a_0 = 0$ can be transformed by a Tschirnhaus substitution of degree $\leq 4$ into the *Bring normal form* $y^5 + py + q = 0$ — a one-parameter family (since $p$ can be absorbed by rescaling $y$, leaving a single essential parameter). The Tschirnhaus substitution $y = c_4 x^4 + c_3 x^3 + c_2 x^2 + c_1 x + c_0$ has 5 free coefficients $c_0, \ldots, c_4$, and Bring showed that solving the auxiliary equations for these coefficients to eliminate the quartic, cubic, and quadratic terms in $y$ requires only operations of degree $\leq 4$ — i.e. is itself solvable by radicals (since the auxiliary system has Galois group inside $S_4$). Bring's work was lost in the Lund archives until 1864 when Sylvester discovered and publicized it, by which time Jerrard (1859, below) had independently rediscovered the result. The Bring reduction is the *algebraic preprocessing* step that makes Hermite's 1858 modular-function solution of the quintic possible: Hermite solves the Bring form $y^5 - y + t = 0$ in theta constants, and the Bring reduction supplies the preprocessing from the general quintic to this one-parameter form. This places the depth-of-radical-tower for the *Tschirnhaus-reducible part* of the quintic squarely inside the solvable $S_4$-regime classified in this file — the irreducible non-solvable part is then exactly the one-parameter Bring quintic, which requires the escape to modular functions of keyInsight #11. The dual algorithm (Bring's algebraic reduction + Hermite's modular solution) gives a constructive proof that *every* quintic over $\mathbb{Q}$ is solvable in Bring-Jerrard normal form by elliptic-modular functions — not by radicals, exactly as Abel-Ruffini proves here. Cited in keyInsight #11.

references.title: An Essay on the Resolution of Equations
references.note: George Birch Jerrard's independent rediscovery (1832 preliminary, 1859 final) of the Bring reduction (entry above), now standardly called the **Bring-Jerrard normal form**. Jerrard extended Bring's result by attempting to push the Tschirnhaus reduction beyond degree 5 to higher-degree equations, conjecturing (incorrectly) that every degree-$n$ equation could be reduced to a normal form with only $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ or fewer parameters. Hamilton (1836) showed Jerrard's general claim was wrong — only the quintic admits the one-parameter reduction — but the $n = 5$ case stands as the key algebraic preprocessing step in the Hermite-Brioschi-Kronecker solution of the quintic in modular functions (Hermite 1858, reference above). The historical name 'Bring-Jerrard' acknowledges both Bring's 1786 priority (lost in Swedish archives until 1864) and Jerrard's 1859 independent rediscovery and dissemination — the standard accepted convention since Sylvester (1864). Jerrard's *Essay* is the most widely-read primary source for the reduction method in 19th-century English-language algebra; the technique appears in modern textbooks (e.g., King 1996, *Beyond the Quartic Equation*) as the bridge between purely algebraic quintic theory and the modular-function escape. Cited together with Bring (1786) in keyInsight #11.

references.title: Resolution of algebraic equations by theta constants
references.venue: Appendix to D. Mumford, *Tata Lectures on Theta II*, Birkhäuser, pp. 261–272
references.note: Extends Hermite's quintic-by-theta-constants result to arbitrary degree: every polynomial equation of degree $n$ is solvable in *Siegel modular functions* of genus $\leq n - 1$, via the action of $S_n$ on the moduli space of principally polarized abelian varieties of genus $n - 1$. The genus-1 case ($n \leq 4$) reduces to classical elliptic modular functions; the genus-2 case ($n = 5$) is Hermite's theorem; higher genera require the full Siegel theta-constant theory. Establishes that the Abel-Ruffini threshold $n = 4$ is sharp specifically against *radical* solvability, not against closed-form expression in general — every algebraic equation is solvable in theta constants. Cited in keyInsight #11.

references.title: Abel's Theorem in Problems and Solutions, Based on the Lectures of Professor V. I. Arnold
references.venue: Kluwer Academic Publishers (Translated from the Russian by Francesca Aicardi); original Russian edition Nauka 1976
references.note: Definitive transcription and expansion of V. I. Arnold's 1963 Moscow State University lecture course presenting the **topological proof of Abel-Ruffini**. The book reconstructs Arnold's argument via a sequence of ~350 graded problems, leading the reader through complex numbers, fundamental groups, branched coverings, and the braid-group monodromy of the discriminant complement $\mathrm{Conf}_n(\mathbb{C})/S_n$. The culminating Chapter 2 shows that any formula expressing the roots of $x^n + a_1 x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_n$ as a finite tower of radicals must have monodromy in the iterated commutator subgroup $B_n^{(d)}$ of the $n$-strand braid group, and proves that for $n = 5$ the image of $B_5^{(d)}$ in $S_5$ always contains the simple non-abelian group $A_5$ — contradicting solvability. The proof uses *no field theory and no Galois group* — only the topology of $\mathbb{C}^n$ and the algebra of $\pi_1(\mathrm{Conf}_5(\mathbb{C})/S_5) = B_5$. Cited in keyInsight #12 as the canonical alternative route to this file's classical-Galois proof of the $n = 5$ threshold.

references.title: Topological Galois Theory: Solvability and Unsolvability of Equations in Finite Terms
references.venue: Springer Monographs in Mathematics, Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg (xviii + 307 pp.)
references.note: Comprehensive monograph generalizing Arnold's topological proof of Abel-Ruffini into a *topological Galois theory* classifying which closed-form expressions in various function classes — radical, elementary, Liouvillian, Pfaffian — are admissible for solving algebraic and differential equations. Khovanskii's framework replaces the field-theoretic Galois group with the *monodromy group* of the resolvent covering and characterizes solvability by the structure (solvable, virtually solvable, abelian-by-finite) of this monodromy group. Major theorems: (1) Arnold's topological Abel-Ruffini ($A_5$ obstruction via braid monodromy) — the model case formalized via Alekseev (2004); (2) topological proof that the integral $\int e^{-x^2} dx$ has no elementary antiderivative (Liouville's theorem); (3) Khovanskii's own theorem that fewnomial equations admit at most a bounded-by-monomial-count number of solutions, generalizing Bézout's theorem. Together with Alekseev (2004), provides the modern textbook reference for the topological/monodromic approach to solvability obstructions complementing the field-theoretic Galois-group approach formalized in this file. Cited in keyInsight #12.

references.title: Moderne Algebra
references.venue: Springer, Berlin (Vol. I, xiii + 243 pp.); English translation *Algebra*, Ungar 1949, reprinted Springer GTM 1991
references.note: The canonical textbook source for the theorem that the Galois group of the *generic* degree-$n$ polynomial $f(X) = X^n - e_1 X^{n-1} + \cdots + (-1)^n e_n$ over the field of symmetric functions $K = k(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ is the full symmetric group $S_n$, acting by permuting the algebraically independent indeterminate roots $t_1, \ldots, t_n$. Van der Waerden codified this fact — implicit in Galois's 1832 memoir — as the bridge that turns the *group-theoretic* solvability classification of this file ($S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$) into the *analytic* Abel-Ruffini statement (the general quintic is unsolvable by radicals). The 1930 first edition (Vol. I, §59 'Die allgemeine Gleichung n-ten Grades') is the modern algebra textbook that established the Galois-theoretic framework as the standard expository route to Abel-Ruffini, eclipsing the earlier Lagrange-resolvent presentations. Cited in keyInsight #13 ('The generic Galois group is $S_n$').

references.title: Topics in Galois Theory
references.venue: Research Notes in Mathematics, Vol. 1, Jones and Bartlett Publishers (xv + 117 pp.); 2nd edition A K Peters / CRC Press 2007
references.note: Definitive modern treatment of **Hilbert's irreducibility theorem** (Chapter 3, 'Hilbert's irreducibility theorem'): for any irreducible $f(T, X) \in \mathbb{Q}(T)[X]$, the set of $t_0 \in \mathbb{Q}$ for which the specialization $f(t_0, X) \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$ remains irreducible is the complement of a *thin set* (Serre's terminology, formalized in §3.1) — thin sets have natural density $0$, so 'almost all' rational specializations preserve irreducibility, and in particular preserve the Galois group. Combined with the generic-Galois-group theorem (van der Waerden 1930), this descent makes Abel-Ruffini concrete: specializing the coefficients of the generic quintic $X^5 - e_1 X^4 + \cdots - e_5 \in \mathbb{Q}(e_1, \ldots, e_5)[X]$ to rational values preserves the Galois group $S_5$ outside a thin set, so a 'random' rational quintic — e.g. $X^5 - X - 1$ — has Galois group $S_5$ and is unsolvable by radicals. Cited in keyInsight #13 as the descent step from the generic to the rational case.

references.title: Über die Irreduzibilität ganzer rationaler Functionen mit ganzzahligen Coefficienten
references.venue: Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik (Crelle) 110: 104–129
references.note: Hilbert's original **Irreduzibilitätssatz** (irreducibility theorem) — the foundational paper underlying the generic-to-rational descent that turns this file's classification of solvable $S_n$ into a statement about *concrete* rational polynomials. Hilbert proved: if $f(t, X) \in \mathbb{Z}[t, X]$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}(t)[X]$, then there exist *infinitely many* integers $t_0 \in \mathbb{Z}$ for which the specialization $f(t_0, X) \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ remains irreducible — i.e., irreducibility is preserved under 'generic' rational specialization. The proof uses Hilbert's *box principle*: estimating the count of $(t_0, x_0)$ pairs satisfying $f(t_0, x_0) = 0$ via a pigeonhole-style bound on integer points on the affine variety $\{f = 0\}$, with the key inequality derived from the canonical heights of those points. Serre (1992) modernized this into the *thin-set* formulation: the exceptional set of $t_0 \in \mathbb{Q}$ where irreducibility fails is *thin* (of natural density $0$), so 'almost all' specializations preserve the Galois group. **Hilbert's motivation**: §III of the paper explicitly constructs polynomials with Galois group $S_n$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ — the *first* unconditional realization of $S_n$ as a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$ for all $n$, predating the inverse Galois program by 8 years. Hilbert's construction starts from the generic polynomial $X^n - e_1 X^{n-1} + \cdots \pm e_n$ over $\mathbb{Q}(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$, whose Galois group is $S_n$ by van der Waerden's theorem (then implicit, formalized in 1930), and specializes the coefficients $e_j$ to rational values via the Irreduzibilitätssatz. This is the *concrete realization* path complementing Shafarevich's theorem for solvable groups (1954, reference above): for $S_n$ specifically — including the non-solvable $S_5, S_6, \ldots$ pinned as non-solvable in this file — Hilbert's 1892 paper already provided the realization over $\mathbb{Q}$, sharpening Abel-Ruffini's negative impossibility to the *positive* concrete unsolvability of specific rational quintics. **Modern legacy**: Hilbert's 1892 paper is the foundational reference for the entire field of *arithmetic Galois theory*, including the inverse Galois problem (Hilbert's own problem 12 in his 1900 ICM lecture), the regular inverse Galois problem (Fried-Jarden 1986), and the constructive realization of finite simple groups via rigidity (Belyi, Matzat 1984). Cited as the original source behind keyInsight #13's generic-to-rational descent.

references.title: Algebraic matric groups and the Picard-Vessiot theory of homogeneous linear ordinary differential equations
references.note: Foundational paper establishing **differential Galois theory** (Picard-Vessiot theory) in modern algebraic form: for a homogeneous linear ODE $L(y) = 0$ with coefficients in a differential field $(F, \partial)$, the minimal extension containing $n$ linearly independent solutions has a Galois group that is naturally a **linear algebraic group** $G \leq \mathrm{GL}_n(C)$ over the constant field $C$. Kolchin's central theorem: the ODE is *solvable by quadratures* (integrations, exponentials, algebraic operations) iff the connected component $G^\circ$ is a *solvable algebraic group*. This is the precise ODE analogue of Galois's solvability criterion proved in this file's polynomial setting, and the obstruction is structurally identical — non-solvable algebraic groups $\mathrm{SL}_2, \mathrm{SL}_n, \mathrm{PSL}_2$ play the role of non-solvable finite groups $S_n, A_n$ ($n \geq 5$). The $A_5 \hookrightarrow \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ icosahedral embedding makes the connection sharp: the same $A_5$ that obstructs polynomial solvability obstructs the integrability of icosahedral hypergeometric equations and certain Lamé equations. Cited in keyInsight #14.

references.title: Lectures on Differential Galois Theory
references.venue: University Lecture Series, Vol. 7, American Mathematical Society (xiii + 105 pp.)
references.note: Standard modern textbook on Picard-Vessiot theory and differential Galois groups. Develops the parallel with classical Galois theory in full detail: differential fields, differential automorphisms, the Picard-Vessiot extension as the differential analogue of a splitting field, and the fundamental theorem giving the bijection between intermediate differential fields and closed subgroups of the differential Galois group. Includes the Tannakian-categorical interpretation that unifies classical and differential Galois theory (Deligne 1990, *Catégories tannakiennes*) and is the entry point for the formalization frontier referenced in keyInsight #14: a Lean implementation of Picard-Vessiot theory would parallel Mathlib's `IsGalois` infrastructure but with `LinearAlgebraicGroup` in place of finite group, and `Derivation` in place of field homomorphism.

references.title: An algorithm for solving second order linear homogeneous differential equations
references.note: Decision algorithm for the Picard-Vessiot solvability of second-order ODEs $y'' = r(x) y$ with $r \in \mathbb{Q}(x)$. Returns the explicit Liouvillian solution (algebraic + integration + exponentiation) if and only if the differential Galois group is solvable, by enumerating the four possible solvable cases: (1) cyclic, (2) dihedral, (3) tetrahedral $A_4$, (4) octahedral $S_4$. The fifth Platonic case — *icosahedral $A_5$* — is non-solvable and is exactly the obstruction proved here as this file's central lemma. Kovacic's algorithm is the *constructive computational counterpart* to this file's qualitative classification, implemented in Maple, Mathematica, Sage, and Magma; given any second-order linear ODE with rational coefficients, it decides solvability in polynomial time in the input size. Cited in keyInsight #14 as the algorithmic face of the differential Galois obstruction.

references.title: Ueber diejenigen Fälle, in welchen die Gaussische hypergeometrische Reihe eine algebraische Function ihres vierten Elementes darstellt
references.venue: Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik (Crelle) 75: 292–335
references.note: Schwarz's complete classification of the cases in which Gauss's hypergeometric series $\,_2F_1(a, b; c; z)$ is an *algebraic* function of $z$ — equivalently, the cases in which the Riemann hypergeometric differential equation $z(1-z) y'' + (c - (a+b+1)z) y' - ab\, y = 0$ has *finite* differential Galois group. Schwarz exhibits 15 explicit parameter families $(a, b, c)$, organized by the underlying finite subgroup of $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$: cyclic, dihedral, tetrahedral ($A_4$), octahedral ($S_4$), and **icosahedral ($A_5$)** — the same five Platonic-symmetry groups that this file's solvability threshold $n \leq 4$ singles out, with the icosahedral $A_5$ case being the *minimal non-solvable* hypergeometric instance. Schwarz's list (now called the *Schwarz list*) gives the explicit algebraic solutions in each case, deriving them from the *triangle-tessellation* picture: solutions correspond to conformal maps from the upper half-plane to spherical/Euclidean/hyperbolic triangles with vertex angles $\pi/p, \pi/q, \pi/r$ where $(p, q, r)$ is a *Platonic triple* $(2, 2, n), (2, 3, 3), (2, 3, 4), (2, 3, 5)$. The icosahedral case $(2, 3, 5)$ — corresponding to $A_5$ — gives Klein's icosahedral solutions cited in keyInsight #6 and the icosahedral form of the quintic systematized in Klein's 1884 *Vorlesungen über das Ikosaeder*. Schwarz's 1873 classification is the *first complete decision* of an algebraic-solvability question via differential Galois theory (avant la lettre — Picard-Vessiot was 25 years later) and is the direct ancestor of Kovacic's algorithm (1986, next reference but one): Kovacic systematized Schwarz's enumeration into a decision procedure for second-order ODEs with rational coefficients. Cited in keyInsight #14 ('Riemann hypergeometric equation has solvability classified by Schwarz (1873) into 15 explicit cases').

references.title: On second order linear differential equations with algebraic solutions
references.note: Classification of second-order linear ODEs on an elliptic curve (Lamé equations $y'' = (n(n+1)\wp(x) + B) y$) whose solutions are *algebraic* — equivalently, whose differential Galois group is *finite*. The finite subgroups of $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ are exactly the five Platonic symmetry groups: cyclic, dihedral, tetrahedral $A_4$, octahedral $S_4$, icosahedral $A_5$ — precisely the groups whose solvability is classified by this file's threshold $n \leq 4$. Baldassarri-Dwork's icosahedral case (Lamé equation with $A_5$ Galois group) is the *minimal non-solvable Lamé*, mirroring the role of $S_5$-quintics as the minimal non-radical-solvable polynomials. Together with Klein's *Vorlesungen über das Ikosaeder* (1884, already referenced), establishes the icosahedron as the universal locus of $A_5$-symmetry across polynomial, ODE, modular, and topological frameworks. Cited in keyInsight #14.

references.title: Theorie der Abel'schen Zahlkörper
references.note: First complete proof of the **Kronecker-Weber theorem**: every finite abelian Galois extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is contained in a cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ for some primitive $n$-th root of unity. The smallest such $n$ is the *conductor* of $K$. Kronecker had announced the result in 1853 (*Über die algebraisch auflösbaren Gleichungen*, Monatsbericht der Königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin), but his proof contained a gap in the $2$-power case; Weber's 1886 paper supplied the first rigorous argument. Hilbert (1896, §136 of the *Zahlbericht*) gave the streamlined modern proof using ramification theory at primes ramified in $K/\mathbb{Q}$. The theorem is the **abelian special case of the inverse Galois problem** — fully resolved a century before Shafarevich's solvable case (1954). Combined with this file's classification of solvable $S_n$ ($n \leq 4$), Kronecker-Weber recipes the abelian composition factors $\mathbb{Z}/2$, $\mathbb{Z}/3$, $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ as Galois groups of explicit subfields of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_4)$, $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_7)$, $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{24})$. Cited in conclusion implication #8.

references.title: Die Theorie der algebraischen Zahlkörper (Zahlbericht)
references.venue: Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung 4: 175–546; English translation *The Theory of Algebraic Number Fields*, Springer 1998 (Lemmermeyer-Schappacher transl.)
references.note: Hilbert's comprehensive 1897 *Zahlbericht* (Report on Algebraic Number Fields) synthesized the prior 30 years of algebraic number theory — Kummer, Kronecker, Dedekind, Weber — into a single coherent framework, and provided the modern textbook proof of the Kronecker-Weber theorem (§136). Hilbert's proof reduces the abelian-over-$\mathbb{Q}$ case to two structural facts: (i) the ramification at a prime $p$ in an abelian extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is bounded by the tame and wild ramification structure of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q}$, and (ii) every cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ has Galois group $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ — itself a *concrete* abelian group whose subfields exhaust all abelian extensions ramified only at primes dividing $n$. Hilbert posed the **inverse Galois problem** (problem 12 in his 1900 ICM lecture) as the next frontier: extend Kronecker-Weber from abelian to arbitrary finite Galois groups by finding explicit *modular* or *automorphic* generators for the non-abelian case — a problem still open in 2026. Cited in conclusion implication #8.

references.title: Über eine Theorie des relativ Abel'schen Zahlkörpers
references.venue: Journal of the College of Science, Imperial University of Tokyo 41(9): 1–133
references.note: Takagi's foundational paper extending Kronecker-Weber from $\mathbb{Q}$ to arbitrary number fields — the birth of **class field theory**. Takagi (then 45) proved: for any number field $K$ and any modulus $\mathfrak{m}$ (a formal product of primes and infinite places), there is a canonical bijection between (a) finite abelian extensions $L/K$ unramified outside $\mathfrak{m}$ and (b) subgroups of finite index in the *ray class group* $\mathrm{Cl}_K^\mathfrak{m}$, with $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K) \cong \mathrm{Cl}_K^\mathfrak{m}/N_{L/K}\mathrm{Cl}_L^\mathfrak{m}$ in the bijection. Specialized to $K = \mathbb{Q}$, this recovers Kronecker-Weber (every abelian extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ sits inside a cyclotomic field) since $\mathrm{Cl}_\mathbb{Q}^{(n)} \cong (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times = \mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q})$. Artin (1927) refined the bijection by adding the reciprocity isomorphism via Frobenius elements; Chevalley (1936) reformulated everything in terms of *idèles* — yielding the modern adelic class field theory. The Takagi-Artin-Chevalley framework is the *complete* solution to the abelian inverse Galois problem over any number field, sharply contrasting with the *open* state of the non-abelian inverse Galois problem over $\mathbb{Q}$ that Hilbert's problem 12 still asks. Cited in conclusion implication #8.

references.title: Solution of Polynomials by Real Radicals
references.note: Isaacs' clean Galois-theoretic proof of **Cardano's casus irreducibilis**: a real algebraic number $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ is expressible by a finite tower of *real* radicals over $\mathbb{Q}$ — i.e. $\mathbb{Q} \subseteq K_1 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq K_r \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ with each $K_{i+1} = K_i(\sqrt[n_i]{a_i})$ for some positive real $a_i \in K_i$ — *if and only if* the Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(N/\mathbb{Q})$ of the Galois closure $N \supseteq \mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ is a **$2$-group** (order a power of $2$). The proof uses elementary Kummer theory: the only $n$-th roots of unity contained in $\mathbb{R}$ are $\{\pm 1\}$, so for $n_i$ odd the extension $K_i(\sqrt[n_i]{a_i})/K_i$ is forced to be trivial after the cyclotomic ascent, and only $n_i = 2$ contributes a nontrivial Galois factor. Specialized to irreducible cubics: $\mathrm{Gal}(f/\mathbb{Q}) \in \{A_3, S_3\}$ for any irreducible cubic, with orders $3$ and $6$ — neither a $2$-power — so any cubic with three real roots is *not* expressible by real radicals, despite its splitting field being entirely real. This sharpens this file's $S_n$-solvable classification: Abel-Ruffini at $n \leq 4$ proves $\mathbb{C}$-radical-solvability; the Isaacs $2$-group criterion carves out a strictly finer $\mathbb{R}$-radical-solvability boundary inside the solvable regime. Cardano's 1545 discovery of the casus irreducibilis is thereby pinned as the *minimal evidence* that the real number system is algebraically incomplete in a precise Galois-theoretic sense — anticipating the systematic introduction of $\mathbb{C}$ in Bombelli's *L'Algebra* (1572). Refinements: Albu (*J. Algebra* 137(1): 1–11, 1991) gave a cleaner Kummer-theoretic proof, and Roth (*Math. Mag.* 63(4): 254–262, 1990) provided the pedagogically clearest presentation. Cited in keyInsight #15.

references.title: Galois extensions of a maximal cyclotomic field
references.venue: Izvestiya Akademii Nauk SSSR. Seriya Matematicheskaya 43(2): 267–276; English translation in Mathematics of the USSR-Izvestiya 14(2): 247–256 (1980)
references.note: **Belyi's theorem**: every smooth projective algebraic curve $X$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ admits a meromorphic function $\beta: X \to \mathbb{P}^1_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}$ — a **Belyi map** — branched only over $\{0, 1, \infty\}$. This unifies the arithmetic and geometric perspectives on Galois covers: curves defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ are precisely those admitting a covering structure governed by the *three-string braid group* $\pi_1(\mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \{0, 1, \infty\}) = \hat F_2$ (the profinite free group on 2 generators), and the absolute Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ acts faithfully on the corresponding **dessins d'enfants** (Grothendieck 1984, *Esquisse d'un programme*). Belyi's proof is elementary and constructive: given any non-constant rational function $f: X \to \mathbb{P}^1$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, iteratively compose with polynomials of the form $z \mapsto \frac{m^m n^n}{(m+n)^{m+n}} z^m (1-z)^n$ until the branching is concentrated at $\{0, 1, \infty\}$ — the construction terminates in $O(\log \deg f)$ steps. **Application to the regular inverse Galois problem for $A_n$**: combined with rigidity theory (Thompson 1984, below), Belyi's construction produces explicit regular Galois covers of $\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Q}}$ with Galois group $A_n$ for all $n \geq 4$, using rigid triples of permutations in $A_n$ satisfying $\sigma_0 \sigma_1 \sigma_\infty = 1$. The connection to this file's classification is structural: the *generic* Galois group $A_n$ (for the unbranched generic cover) is realized regularly via the *three-point* Belyi map, with the $A_5$-rigid-triple case ($\sigma_0 = (12345)$, $\sigma_1 = (12)(34)$, $\sigma_\infty = (13524)$) corresponding to the **icosahedral** dessin and the smallest non-abelian simple regular cover of $\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Q}}$. Cited in the openQuestion on regular inverse Galois problem.

references.title: Some finite groups which appear as $\mathrm{Gal}\,L/K$, where $K \subseteq \mathbb{Q}(\mu_n)$
references.note: Thompson's **rigidity criterion** for the regular inverse Galois problem: a finite group $G$ is realizable as $\mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q}(t))$ with $L \cap \overline{\mathbb{Q}} = \mathbb{Q}$ (regular Galois extension) provided $G$ admits a **rigid triple** of generators — three conjugacy classes $C_1, C_2, C_3 \subset G$ such that the set $\{(g_1, g_2, g_3) : g_i \in C_i,\ g_1 g_2 g_3 = 1,\ \langle g_1, g_2, g_3\rangle = G\}$ consists of a single $G$-conjugacy class, and the classes are *$\mathbb{Q}$-rational* (preserved by the absolute Galois action on the character table). The geometric content: rigidity guarantees a single isomorphism class of three-point branched covers of $\mathbb{P}^1$ with monodromy $G$ and ramification classes $(C_1, C_2, C_3)$, and rationality of the classes plus rigidity descends the cover to $\mathbb{Q}(t)$. Thompson's landmark application: the **monster group** $M$ (largest sporadic simple group, order $\approx 8 \times 10^{53}$) is RIGP-realizable, established via a rigid triple of elements of orders 2, 3, 29 in $M$. Thompson's method extended to **24 of the 26 sporadic simple groups** (the exceptions being the Mathieu groups $M_{23}$ and one other), making rigidity the most powerful single technique for the regular inverse Galois problem. **Connection to this file**: Thompson's rigidity for $A_n$ via three-point Belyi covers (Belyi 1979, above) gives the geometric face of the IGP-realizability of $A_n$ that complements this file's classification of which $A_n$ are *solvable* (the answer here: $n \leq 4$ for solvability; all $n \geq 4$ for RIGP-realizability via rigid triples — the two thresholds are distinct because non-solvable RIGP-realization is possible). Cited in the openQuestion on regular inverse Galois problem.

references.title: Gleichungen mit vorgeschriebener Gruppe
references.note: Emmy Noether's foundational paper posing what is now called **Noether's problem**: given a finite group $G \leq S_n$ acting on $K(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ by permuting indeterminates, is the fixed field $K(x_1, \ldots, x_n)^G$ purely transcendental over $K$? A positive answer for $G$ over $K = \mathbb{Q}$ gives an explicit parametric family of $G$-Galois extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$ (via Hilbert irreducibility), sharpening the abstract inverse-Galois existence to constructive realization. Noether resolved the question affirmatively for $G = S_n$ (the fixed field is $\mathbb{Q}(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ by the fundamental theorem of symmetric functions) — the structural source of the file's classification of solvable $S_n$ acquiring a parametric companion via van der Waerden's generic-Galois-group theorem (1930). The general question was *open* in Noether's day for all non-symmetric groups and remains *open* in 2026 for general finite groups, despite the negative resolutions of Swan (1969) for $G = \mathbb{Z}/47$ and Lenstra (1974) for general abelian groups. Cited in openQuestion #11.

references.title: Invariant rational functions and a problem of Steenrod
references.note: **First negative answer to Noether's problem**: Richard Swan proved that for $G = \mathbb{Z}/47\mathbb{Z}$ acting on $\mathbb{Q}(x_1, \ldots, x_{47})$ by cyclic permutation, the fixed field $\mathbb{Q}(x_1, \ldots, x_{47})^G$ is *not* purely transcendental over $\mathbb{Q}$. The obstruction is a non-trivial element of the unramified Brauer group $\mathrm{Br}_{\mathrm{nr}}(\mathbb{Q}(x_1, \ldots, x_{47})^G/\mathbb{Q})$, which by purity is invariant under stable rational equivalence. Swan's choice of $p = 47$ is dictated by the irregularity of the prime $47$ for the cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{47})$: the class number $h(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{47}))^+$ contains a non-trivial $47$-torsion element that descends to the unramified Brauer obstruction. This paper established that Noether's problem has a *strictly negative* general answer, even for cyclic groups, and motivated the systematic study of *stable rationality* and the *Bogomolov multiplier* $\mathrm{B}_0(G)$ as the precise obstruction. Cited in openQuestion #11.

references.title: Rational functions invariant under a finite abelian group
references.note: **Complete classification of Noether's problem for abelian groups over $\mathbb{Q}$**: Hendrik Lenstra proved that for a finite abelian group $G$, the fixed field $\mathbb{Q}(x_1, \ldots, x_n)^G$ (with $G$ acting by regular permutation on $|G| = n$ indeterminates) is purely transcendental over $\mathbb{Q}$ iff $G$ satisfies an explicit *cyclotomic criterion* expressible via class group computations in $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$. The criterion fails for infinitely many cyclic groups, including $\mathbb{Z}/8$ (the smallest such) and $\mathbb{Z}/47$ (Swan 1969, above), making Lenstra's theorem the *definitive boundary* of Noether-rationality in the abelian case: cyclic groups of prime order $p$ are Noether-rational iff $p$ is *regular* in Kummer's sense ($p \nmid h(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p))^+$). For non-abelian groups the question remains *wide open* in 2026 — the major outstanding case being $p$-groups of nilpotency class $\geq 3$, where the Bogomolov multiplier $\mathrm{B}_0(G)$ provides examples on both sides of the dividing line (Saltman 1984, Bogomolov 1988). Cited in openQuestion #11.

references.title: Extensions régulières de $\mathbb{Q}(T)$ de groupe de Galois $\tilde{A}_n$
references.note: Jean-François Mestre's constructive realization of $A_n$ and its double cover $\tilde{A}_n$ as regular Galois groups over $\mathbb{Q}(t)$ for *all* $n$, with the underlying Noether-rational witness: the fixed field $\mathbb{Q}(x_1, \ldots, x_n)^{A_n}$ is purely transcendental over $\mathbb{Q}$, generated by the elementary symmetric polynomials $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ together with the discriminant square root $\delta = \prod_{i < j}(x_i - x_j)$. This *positively* resolves Noether's problem for $A_n$ across all $n$ — the alternating analogue of Noether's 1918 resolution for $S_n$ — and provides explicit *parametric families* of $A_n$-Galois extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$ extending van der Waerden's $S_n$-recipe. Mestre's construction is the constructive face of this file's qualitative classification: $A_n$ is solvable for $n \leq 4$ (proved here) *and* Noether-rational for all $n$ (proved by Mestre), so for $n \leq 4$ the file's solvability classification is realized by *both* radical formulas (Cardano-Ferrari) and Mestre's parametric recipe, while for $n \geq 5$ the parametric recipe persists even though the radical recipe is blocked by Abel-Ruffini. Cited in openQuestion #11.

references.title: Bildung zusammengesetzter Gruppen
references.note: Otto Hölder's foundational paper establishing the structure of finite groups in terms of their composition factors — the source of the **Jordan-Hölder theorem** (uniqueness of composition factors up to permutation, cited by sub-entry `abel-ruffini-galois-extensions-oq-04`) and the first systematic computation of the automorphism groups $\mathrm{Aut}(S_n)$ for the symmetric-group family. Hölder proved: $\mathrm{Aut}(S_n) \cong S_n$ for all $n \neq 2, 6$ (via the action of $S_n$ on itself by conjugation, which is the *inner* automorphism group $\mathrm{Inn}(S_n) \cong S_n$ for $n \geq 3$ since the center is trivial), and the *exceptional* case $\mathrm{Aut}(S_6) \cong S_6 \rtimes \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ with $|\mathrm{Out}(S_6)| = 2$ — the **unique non-trivial outer automorphism among all symmetric groups**. Hölder's proof technique for $\mathrm{Out}(S_6) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ relies on the *two non-conjugate classes* of order-120 subgroups in $S_6$ — the intransitive point-stabilizers ($\cong S_5$ acting on 5 points) and the transitive $\mathrm{PGL}_2(5)$-copies acting on 6 cosets of a Sylow 5-subgroup — building on Sylvester's 1844 *duads and synthemes* combinatorics. The theorem $\mathrm{Out}(S_n) = \{e\}$ for $n \neq 2, 6$ is the structural reason the $S_n$ family is 'rigid' across all but one exceptional point, and the exceptional outer automorphism at $n = 6$ is the *deepest single source* of the sporadic finite simple groups (via the Mathieu chain $M_{12} \hookrightarrow M_{24} \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Co}_0 \hookrightarrow M$ — see cross-reference `inverse-galois-oq-02`). Cited in keyInsight #16.

references.title: The Brauer group of quotient spaces by linear group actions
references.venue: Izvestiya Akademii Nauk SSSR. Seriya Matematicheskaya 30(3): 455–485; English translation in Mathematics of the USSR-Izvestiya 30(3): 455–485 (1988)
references.note: Fedor Bogomolov's definitive obstruction theory for Noether's problem in the $p$-group case: the **Bogomolov multiplier** $\mathrm{B}_0(G) = \ker\!\big(H^2(G, \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}) \to \prod_A H^2(A, \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})\big)$ (where $A$ ranges over *bicyclic* subgroups of $G$) is a quotient of the Schur multiplier by 'toral classes' and equals the unramified Brauer group $\mathrm{Br}_{\mathrm{nr}}(K(G)/K)$ for $K$ algebraically closed of characteristic $0$. **Theorem**: $\mathrm{B}_0(G) \neq 0 \Rightarrow K(x_1, \ldots, x_n)^G$ is *not* stably rational, hence not purely transcendental, hence Noether-negative for $G$. Bogomolov gave the first non-cyclic counterexamples to Noether's problem (specifically certain finite $p$-groups of nilpotency class 2 with non-trivial Bogomolov multiplier), establishing that Noether-negativity is *generic* among $p$-groups rather than exceptional. The theorem builds on Saltman (1984, *Noether's problem over an algebraically closed field*, Invent. Math. 77: 71–84), who introduced the unramified-Brauer-group obstruction in the algebraically closed setting. Cited in openQuestion #11.

references.title: The determination of Galois groups
references.note: **Stauduhar's algorithm** — the canonical decision procedure for computing $\mathrm{Gal}(f/\mathbb{Q})$ as a specific transitive subgroup of $S_n$ for an irreducible $f \in \mathbb{Q}[X]$ of degree $n$. The algorithm performs a **subgroup-lattice descent**: enumerate the transitive subgroups $H \leq S_n$ from $S_n$ downward and at each step build a **resolvent polynomial** $R_H(X) = \prod_{T_i \in S_n/H}(X - T_i \cdot \theta)$ for a Galois-invariant test polynomial $\theta \in \mathbb{Q}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ stabilized exactly by $H$; numerical evaluation at high-precision approximate roots followed by exact rational reconstruction certifies $\mathrm{Gal}(f) \subseteq H$ up to conjugacy iff $R_H$ has a rational root. The depth of the descent equals the maximal chain length in the transitive-subgroup lattice of $S_n$ — bounded by $\mathrm{dl}(S_n)$ in the solvable regime, exploding to $\Omega(\log n)$ at the non-solvable threshold $n = 5$ proved here as the file's central lemma. Implemented in PARI/GP (`nfgaloisconj`), Magma (`GaloisGroup`), Sage (`f.galois_group()`), Maple (`galois`), and the LMFDB curated query interface (lmfdb.org). The transitive subgroup tables of $S_n$ underlying every implementation were enumerated by Butler-McKay (1983) and Soicher (1985) for $n \leq 15$, Hulpke (2005) for $n \leq 30$, and Cannon-Holt (2008) for $n \leq 47$. Stauduhar's method is the *constructive shadow* of this file's qualitative classification: the threshold $n \leq 4$ proved here pins exactly where the descent terminates in $O(1)$ steps versus enters the simple-composition-factor regime. Cited in keyInsight #17 as the computational engine of modern polynomial Galois theory.

sections.title: Module Header: Imports and Proof Architecture
sections.summary: Five Mathlib imports form a dependency hierarchy: `AbelRuffini` (field theory + radical solvability), `Solvable` (IsSolvable predicate and solvable_of_ker_le_range), `Alternating` (alternating groups and A₅ simplicity), `Galois.Basic` (IsGalois and card_aut_eq_finrank), and `Perm.Sign` (sign homomorphism). The module docstring announces a 15-section structure proving S_n solvable ↔ n ≤ 4 from first principles, extending the simpler AbelRuffini.lean.
sections.mathContext: The proof rests on five Mathlib pillars. `Mathlib.FieldTheory.AbelRuffini` supplies `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`: if $\alpha$ is solvable by radicals over $F$ and is a root of an irreducible $q$, then $\mathrm{Gal}(q)$ is solvable — the field-theoretic half of Galois's criterion. `Mathlib.GroupTheory.Solvable` provides the `IsSolvable G` typeclass (the derived series $G^{(k)}$ eventually reaches $1$) and the splicing lemma `solvable_of_ker_le_range`: from a short exact sequence $1 \to N \to G \to Q \to 1$ with $N$ and $Q$ solvable, conclude $G$ solvable. This file supplies the *group-theoretic* half — exactly which $S_n$ are solvable — which combines with the field-theoretic half to yield Abel–Ruffini.

sections.title: Small Symmetric Groups: S₀–S₄ Solvable
sections.summary: Proves $S_0, S_1$ solvable by subsingleton; $S_2$ by commutativity; $S_3$ via the exact sequence $1 \to A_3 \to S_3 \to \mathbb{Z}^\times \to 1$; $S_4$ via the Klein four-group $V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4$ and the extension $1 \to A_4 \to S_4 \to \mathbb{Z}^\times \to 1$. Also proves $A_0$–$A_4$ solvable.
sections.mathContext: Solvability is built up the chain $S_0,\dots,S_4$ using the extension lemma `solvable_of_ker_le_range` applied to the sign sequence $1 \to A_n \to S_n \xrightarrow{\mathrm{sgn}} \{\pm 1\} \to 1$. $S_0, S_1$ are trivial (`Unique`, hence `isSolvable_of_subsingleton`); $S_2 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ and $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$ are abelian (`isSolvable_of_comm`). The crux is $A_4$, which is *not* abelian: solvability comes from the tower $1 \trianglelefteq V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4$, where $V_4 = \{e,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$ is the Klein four-group (the normal Sylow-2 subgroup of $A_4$) with $A_4/V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$. Both $V_4$ and the quotient are abelian, so two applications of the extension lemma give $A_4$, then $S_4$, solvable. $V_4$ is built explicitly as the `Subgroup` $\{x : x^2 = 1\}$, with normality discharged by `native_decide`.

sections.title: Sharp Threshold: S_n Solvable ↔ n ≤ 4
sections.summary: Proves the complete biconditional: $S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$. Uses `interval_cases n <;> infer_instance` for $n \leq 4$ and Mathlib's `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` for $n \geq 5$.
sections.mathContext: The biconditional $\mathrm{IsSolvable}(S_n) \iff n \le 4$. The $n \ge 5$ direction reduces to Mathlib's `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable`, which needs the cardinality bound $5 \le \#(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)$ (recast through `Cardinal.mk_fintype`). The $n \le 4$ direction is the finite case split `interval_cases n <;> infer_instance`, each instance having been registered in Part I. This is the sharp group-theoretic threshold underlying Abel–Ruffini: $n = 4$ is exactly the largest degree for which the symmetric group — and hence the generic Galois group of a degree-$n$ polynomial — is solvable.

sections.title: A₅: The Minimal Obstruction and Galois Connection
sections.summary: Proves $A_5$ is simple (`alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`), verifies $|A_5| = 60$, and formalizes Galois's contrapositive: non-solvable Galois group implies the polynomial is not solvable by radicals. Also proves Galois group order = extension degree.
sections.mathContext: $A_5$ is the *minimal obstruction*: the smallest non-abelian simple group, of order $60$. Simplicity (`alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`) means its only normal subgroups are $\{e\}$ and $A_5$, so its derived series is constant at $A_5 \ne 1$ — it is non-solvable, and it appears as a composition factor of every $S_n$ with $n \ge 5$. The radical-solvability bridge `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_galois` is the contrapositive of Galois's criterion: for irreducible $q$ with root $\alpha$, if $\mathrm{Gal}(q)$ is not solvable then $\alpha$ is not solvable by radicals. Together with `galois_group_order` ($\#\mathrm{Aut}(E/F) = [E:F]$ for a finite Galois extension, i.e. `IsGalois.card_aut_eq_finrank`), this is the precise hinge translating group non-solvability into the impossibility of a radical formula.

sections.title: Part VI: Subgroup Solvability
sections.summary: Proves that subgroups of solvable groups are solvable via `inferInstance` — a single-keyword proof demonstrating Lean's typeclass hierarchy: $H \leq G$, $G$ solvable $\Rightarrow H$ solvable (derived series of $H$ contained in that of $G$). Used implicitly throughout to conclude $A_n \leq S_n$ solvable whenever $S_n$ is solvable.
sections.mathContext: If $G$ is solvable and $H \le G$, then $H$ is solvable, because the derived series satisfies $H^{(k)} \le G^{(k)}$ for all $k$, so $G^{(n)} = 1$ forces $H^{(n)} = 1$. In Lean this is a Mathlib instance found by `inferInstance` — the one-keyword proof witnessing that solvability is *hereditary* downward. This closure property is used silently wherever the file concludes that $A_n \le S_n$ is solvable from $S_n$ solvable (e.g. `alternating_solvable_of_le_four`).

sections.title: Part VII: Alternating Group Non-Solvability Classification
sections.summary: Proves $A_n$ not solvable for $n \geq 5$ (by contradiction: $A_n$ solvable would imply $S_n$ solvable via `solvable_of_ker_le_range`, contradicting `symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le`). Proves $A_n$ solvable for $n \leq 4$ (subgroup of solvable $S_n$). Assembles the complete biconditional `alternating_solvable_iff`: $A_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$.
sections.mathContext: The alternating analogue of the sharp threshold: $\mathrm{IsSolvable}(A_n) \iff n \le 4$. Non-solvability for $n \ge 5$ is by contradiction — were $A_n$ solvable, the sign sequence $1 \to A_n \to S_n \to \{\pm 1\} \to 1$ with `solvable_of_ker_le_range` would make $S_n$ solvable, contradicting `symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le`. Solvability for $n \le 4$ is downward heredity: $A_n \le S_n$ and $S_n$ is solvable. Note the logical routing: rather than deriving non-solvability directly from $A_5 \le A_n$, the proof goes through $S_n$, reusing the already-established symmetric threshold.

sections.title: Part VIII: Group Cardinalities — $|S_n| = n!$ and $|A_n| = n!/2$
sections.summary: Verifies $|S_2|=2, |S_3|=6, |S_4|=24, |S_5|=120, |S_6|=720$ and $|A_0|=|A_1|=|A_2|=1, |A_3|=3, |A_4|=12, |A_5|=60, |A_6|=360$ computationally. Uses `decide` for small groups and `native_decide` for $S_6$ and $A_6$ (720 and 360 elements exceed kernel evaluation budget). Anchors the $|S_n| = n!$ and $|A_n| = n!/2$ identities as verified facts.
sections.mathContext: Order computations $|S_n| = n!$ and $|A_n| = n!/2$ verified by reflection. `decide` evaluates `Fintype.card` inside the Lean kernel for small $n$ (up to $|S_5| = 120$, $|A_5| = 60$); `native_decide` compiles to native code for $|S_6| = 720$ and $|A_6| = 360$, which exceed the kernel's reduction budget. These are not mere sanity checks: $|A_5| = 60$ is the order of the smallest non-abelian simple group, and the relation $|S_n| = 2|A_n|$ is exactly the index identity $[S_n : A_n] = 2$ — the statement that $A_n = \ker(\mathrm{sgn})$ has index $2$, the structural fact powering every sign-sequence argument.

sections.title: Part IX: Solvability Preservation — Quotients and Isomorphisms
sections.summary: Proves solvability is preserved under quotient groups ($G/N$ solvable whenever $G$ solvable, via `inferInstance`) and isomorphic groups ($G \cong H$, $G$ solvable $\Rightarrow H$ solvable via `solvable_of_surjective`). Together with subgroup solvability (Part VI), these three closure properties — subgroups, quotients, isomorphisms — make solvability a robust hereditary invariant under the Galois correspondence.
sections.mathContext: Two further closure properties completing the trio (with subgroups, Part VI): quotients ($G$ solvable $\Rightarrow G/N$ solvable, since $(G/N)^{(k)}$ is the image of $G^{(k)}$) and isomorphism-invariance ($G \cong H$, $G$ solvable $\Rightarrow H$ solvable via `solvable_of_surjective`, as surjections preserve solvability). Together $\{$subgroup, quotient, surjective image$\}$ make `IsSolvable` a *closed class* — closed under sub, quotient, and extension — which is the abstract characterization of solvable groups and the reason solvability transfers cleanly across the Galois correspondence between subfields and subgroups.

sections.title: Part X: Index and Structure Theorems
sections.summary: Verifies $|S_0|=1$ and $|S_1|=1$ via `decide`, and instantiates `a5_not_solvable` as a named corollary (`alternating_not_solvable_of_five_le le_rfl`) for direct citation by downstream proofs. These three results anchor the cardinality chain at its base cases and provide a canonically named reference to the $A_5$ obstruction.
sections.mathContext: Base-case anchors $|S_0| = |S_1| = 1$ (trivial permutation groups) and a canonically named corollary `a5_not_solvable := alternating_not_solvable_of_five_le le_rfl` exposing the $A_5$ obstruction for direct downstream citation. Naming the $n = 5$ instance separately turns the general $n \ge 5$ theorem into a zero-argument lemma — the cleanest possible reference point for the keystone fact that $A_5$ is not solvable.

sections.title: Part XI: Specific Non-Solvability: S₅–S₈ and A₅–A₇
sections.summary: Concrete non-solvability witnesses for $S_5, S_6, S_7, S_8$ and $A_5, A_6, A_7$ — each a one-liner applying `symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le` or `alternating_not_solvable_of_five_le` with `omega`-computed bounds. Includes `symmetric_not_solvable_of_alternating`: if $A_n$ is not solvable then $S_n$ is not solvable (contrapositive of subgroup solvability, proved immediately by `inferInstance`).
sections.mathContext: Explicit non-solvability instances for $S_5,\dots,S_8$ and $A_5,\dots,A_7$, each obtained by feeding an `omega`-discharged bound $n \ge 5$ into the general thresholds. The structurally interesting result is `symmetric_not_solvable_of_alternating`: $\neg\,\mathrm{IsSolvable}(A_n) \Rightarrow \neg\,\mathrm{IsSolvable}(S_n)$, the contrapositive of downward heredity ($A_n \le S_n$, so $S_n$ solvable would force $A_n$ solvable). It encodes the principle that a non-solvable subgroup obstructs solvability of the whole group — the abstract reason $A_5 \trianglelefteq S_5$ makes $S_5$ non-solvable.

sections.title: Part XII: Chain Properties and Sign Kernel Identity
sections.summary: Proves the commutator subgroup of a solvable group is solvable (`commutator_solvable`), establishes $\ker(\text{sign}) = A_n$ formally (`sign_kernel_is_alternating`), and packages joint solvability of $S_n$ and $A_n$ for $n \leq 4$ (`solvable_small_has_abelian_factors`). The sign kernel identity is the keystone connecting all short exact sequence arguments in the file.
sections.mathContext: Three derived-series and structure facts. `commutator_solvable`: the commutator subgroup $[G,G] = G^{(1)}$ of a solvable group is solvable (its derived series is a tail of $G$'s). `sign_kernel_is_alternating`: $\ker(\mathrm{sgn} : S_n \to \{\pm 1\}) = A_n$, proved by `ext` plus `Equiv.Perm.mem_alternatingGroup` — this is the definitional link tying the alternating group to the sign homomorphism and is what makes every $1 \to A_n \to S_n \to \{\pm 1\} \to 1$ argument well-typed. `solvable_small_has_abelian_factors` bundles solvability of $S_n$ and $A_n$ for $n \le 4$, recording that these groups admit composition series with abelian (indeed cyclic) factors.

sections.title: Part XIII: Non-Commutativity Witnesses
sections.summary: Proves $S_3, S_4, S_5, A_4, A_5$ non-abelian by exhibiting non-commuting element pairs via `push_neg` followed by `decide` (small groups) or `native_decide` (larger groups). Confirms that only $S_1$ and $S_2$ are abelian symmetric groups — a sharp boundary consistent with the solvability classification at $n = 4$.
sections.mathContext: Non-commutativity witnesses obtained by `push_neg` (turning $\neg\,\forall a\,b,\ ab = ba$ into $\exists a\,b,\ ab \ne ba$) then `decide`/`native_decide` to exhibit a concrete non-commuting pair. The boundary is sharp: only $S_0, S_1, S_2$ (and $A_n$ for $n \le 3$) are abelian. Non-commutativity is necessary but not sufficient for non-solvability — $S_3, S_4, A_4$ are non-abelian yet solvable — so these witnesses sit *below* the solvability threshold and illustrate that the genuine obstruction is a non-abelian *simple composition factor* ($A_5$), not mere non-commutativity.

sections.title: Part XIV: Higher Cardinalities — S₇, S₈, A₇, A₈
sections.summary: Verifies $|S_7|=5040, |S_8|=40320, |A_7|=2520, |A_8|=20160$ via `native_decide` (required since $|S_8| = 40320$ elements exceed kernel evaluation budget). Adds explicit non-solvability for $A_6, A_7, A_8$ as one-liners. Notes the exceptional isomorphism $A_8 \cong GL_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ (order 20160) — one of five exceptional isomorphisms between alternating and classical groups discovered during the CFSG.
sections.mathContext: Large-order verifications $|S_7| = 5040$, $|S_8| = 40320$, $|A_7| = 2520$, $|A_8| = 20160$ by `native_decide` (kernel reduction is infeasible at these sizes). The remark $A_8 \cong \mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2) = \mathrm{PSL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ (both order $20160$) is one of the *exceptional isomorphisms* between alternating groups and finite groups of Lie type ($A_5 \cong \mathrm{PSL}_2(4) \cong \mathrm{PSL}_2(5)$, $A_6 \cong \mathrm{PSL}_2(9)$, $A_8 \cong \mathrm{PSL}_4(2)$) — coincidences that vanish for large $n$ and were catalogued during the classification of finite simple groups.

sections.title: Part XV: Factorial Identity Verification ($|S_n| = n!$, $|A_n| = n!/2$)
sections.summary: Proves $|S_n| = n!$ and $|A_n| = n!/2$ as named theorems for $n = 3, 4, 5$ via `decide`. Serves as simp lemmas bridging `Fintype.card` API to `Nat.factorial`, and as regression tests confirming Mathlib's fintype instance for $\text{Equiv.Perm}(\text{Fin } n)$ correctly evaluates to $n!$. The identity $|A_n| = n!/2$ follows from $[S_n : A_n] = 2$ (index of $\ker(\text{sign})$), an application of Lagrange's theorem.
sections.mathContext: The cardinalities recast against `Nat.factorial`: $|S_n| = n!$ and $|A_n| = n!/2$ for $n = 3, 4, 5$. Bridging `Fintype.card (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))` to `Nat.factorial n` makes these usable as `simp` lemmas and as regression tests on Mathlib's fintype instance for permutations. The half-factorial $|A_n| = n!/2$ is the index identity $[S_n : A_n] = 2$ via Lagrange's theorem — $A_n$ is the index-$2$ kernel of the sign map, the cleanest example of a subgroup whose order is forced by its index.

sections.title: Module Summary and Theorem Inventory
sections.summary: Closing docstring inventories 55+ theorems across the 15 sections: solvable small groups ($S_0$–$S_4$, $A_3$–$A_4$), non-solvable large groups ($S_n$, $A_n$ for $n \geq 5$), the two complete biconditionals ($S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$; $A_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$), structural results ($A_5$ simple, $\ker(\text{sign}) = A_n$, cardinalities), non-commutativity witnesses, and preservation theorems. Closes the `AbelRuffiniGaloisExtensions` namespace at line 534, making all results accessible for import.
sections.mathContext: The closing inventory frames the file's contribution: a complete, machine-checked solvability classification of $S_n$ and $A_n$ pinned to the threshold $n = 4$. The two biconditionals $\mathrm{IsSolvable}(S_n) \iff n \le 4$ and $\mathrm{IsSolvable}(A_n) \iff n \le 4$ are the group-theoretic content that, paired with Galois's criterion, yields Abel–Ruffini: the generic polynomial of degree $\ge 5$ has non-solvable Galois group $S_n$ and hence no solution in radicals.

mainTheorems.name: symmetric_solvable_iff
mainTheorems.description: Complete classification: the symmetric group $S_n$ is solvable if and only if $n \leq 4$. The forward direction discharges five cases by `interval_cases n <;> infer_instance` (delegating to the small-$n$ instances built in Part I); the reverse direction packages `symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le` via `by_contra; push_neg; omega`. This is the file's principal contribution to the gallery — the qualitative classification that, paired with Galois's solvability theorem (Mathlib `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`), yields Abel-Ruffini for the generic quintic.

mainTheorems.name: alternating_solvable_iff
mainTheorems.description: The alternating-group analogue: $A_n$ is solvable if and only if $n \leq 4$. The reverse direction follows by subgroup heredity from `symmetric_solvable_iff` ($A_n \leq S_n$); the forward direction goes through the sign-kernel exact sequence — were $A_n$ solvable for $n \geq 5$, then `solvable_of_ker_le_range` applied to the sign exact sequence would make $S_n$ solvable, contradicting the symmetric threshold. Combined with `symmetric_solvable_iff`, this pins the solvability boundary at $n = 4$ from both sides.

mainTheorems.name: a5_simple
mainTheorems.description: $A_5$ is a simple group (no non-trivial normal subgroups). The central obstruction underlying every non-solvability result in the file: $A_5$ simple and non-abelian forces it to appear as a non-cyclic composition factor in $S_n$ for all $n \geq 5$, blocking any abelian-factored composition series. Delegates to Mathlib's `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`, which internally runs the Sylow-counting argument detailed in keyInsight #8 ($n_2 = 5$, $n_3 = 10$, $n_5 = 6$, all $\neq 1$).

mainTheorems.name: not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_galois
mainTheorems.description: Contrapositive of Galois's solvability theorem: if the Galois group of a polynomial is not solvable, then no root is expressible by radicals. Composes Mathlib's `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` (forward direction of Galois's theorem) with negation via `intro hsol; exact hns (... hsol)` — a three-line proof bridging this file's group-theoretic classification (`symmetric_solvable_iff`, `a5_simple`) to the analytic statement of Abel-Ruffini. The named theorem makes the contrapositive directly citable in downstream proofs without unfolding the implication.

mainTheorems.name: sign_kernel_is_alternating
mainTheorems.description: The keystone identity $\ker(\mathrm{sgn} : S_n \to \{\pm 1\}) = A_n$ as a formal equality between subgroups. Proved by `ext` + `Equiv.Perm.mem_alternatingGroup`, this two-line theorem translates the abstract kernel of the sign homomorphism into the concrete alternating subtype and is the linchpin on which every short-exact-sequence argument in Part I pivots — used three times to lift solvability across $1 \to A_n \to S_n \to \mathbb{Z}^\times \to 1$ (for $n = 3, 4$) and $1 \to V_4 \to A_4 \to A_4/V_4 \to 1$.
mainTheorems.leanType: (n : ℕ) : (Equiv.Perm.sign : Equiv.Perm (Fin n) →* ℤˣ).ker = alternatingGroup (Fin n)

mainTheorems.name: galois_group_order
mainTheorems.description: The order of a finite Galois group equals the extension degree: $|\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)| = [E : F]$. Direct invocation of Mathlib's `IsGalois.card_aut_eq_finrank` under the standard hypotheses `[FiniteDimensional F E] [IsGalois F E]`. Establishes the numerical shadow of the Galois correspondence — the bijection between intermediate fields and subgroups in cardinality form — and provides the file's interface to extension degrees from downstream proofs that need to read off $|\mathrm{Gal}|$ from $[E:F]$.
mainTheorems.leanType: [FiniteDimensional F E] [IsGalois F E] : Nat.card (E ≃ₐ[F] E) = Module.finrank F E

mainTheorems.name: solvable_small_has_abelian_factors
mainTheorems.description: Joint solvability packaging for $n \leq 4$: simultaneously certifies $\mathrm{IsSolvable}(S_n)$ AND $\mathrm{IsSolvable}(A_n)$ as a single anonymous-constructor proof $\langle \text{symmetric\_solvable\_of\_le\_four } hn,\ \text{alternating\_solvable\_of\_le\_four } hn\rangle$. While `symmetric_solvable_iff` and `alternating_solvable_iff` give the full biconditional classifications, this paired conjunction is the form most directly consumed by downstream proofs that need *both* solvability witnesses to construct composition series with abelian factors (the canonical $\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_n \trianglelefteq S_n$ tower for $n \leq 4$, refined by $V_4$ at $n = 4$). Flagged as an original contribution in `meta.originalContributions[3]`: bundles two Mathlib instance inferences into a single ergonomic API surface without requiring re-derivation at the call site.
mainTheorems.leanType: (n : ℕ) (hn : n ≤ 4) : IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) ∧ IsSolvable (alternatingGroup (Fin n))
